fun_fact: These tiny toads spend most of the year underground and come out after summer rains.
where_to_find: Desert grasslands and shrublands near temporary pools after heavy rain.
spotting_tip: Listen for a buzzy trill after summer storms and scan damp ground from the trail with a flashlight and an adult.

fun_fact: Whiptails dart around very fast and rarely sit still, which helps them dodge predators.
where_to_find: Dry streambeds, grasslands and desert shrublands with sandy soil.
spotting_tip: Look along sunny, sandy trails and watch for quick striped lizards darting between bushes.

fun_fact: Chipping sparrows often line their nests with soft animal hair, including pet fur.
where_to_find: Lawns, parks, open woodlands and forest edges across most of the country.
spotting_tip: Look for a bird with a rusty cap hopping on lawns and listen for a long, dry trill.

fun_fact: This rare frog lives in mountain streams and ponds and is protected, so seeing one is special.
where_to_find: Clean ponds, streams and stock tanks in mountain canyons of the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Scan pond edges from a distance and never touch the water or frogs; they are protected.

size: Up to 3 ft tall at shoulder (90 cm), 5 ft long (150 cm)
fun_fact: Chital, also called axis deer, keep their white spots for life, unlike many deer fawns.
where_to_find: Grassy fields, forest edges and ranchland where they have been introduced.
spotting_tip: Scan open meadows near forest edges early or late in the day with binoculars.
safety_note: Wild deer can be unpredictable. Use zoom and never feed them.

fun_fact: Male cinnamon teal are a deep reddish-brown with bright red eyes.
where_to_find: Shallow ponds, marshes and wetlands with plenty of plants.
spotting_tip: Look for small, reddish ducks along the edges of marshes and ponds.

fun_fact: A nutcracker can hide tens of thousands of pine seeds each year and remember many of the spots.
where_to_find: Mountain pine forests and high-elevation parks, picnic areas and overlooks.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud, raspy calls in pine trees and look for a gray bird with black-and-white wings.

fun_fact: Spiny lizards do push-ups to show other lizards that a territory is taken.
where_to_find: Rocky hillsides, oak woodlands and canyons in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny rocks and tree trunks from a distance, as they often bask in the open.

fun_fact: Its song sounds like a buzzing insect, with a few flat, buzzy notes in a row.
where_to_find: Prairie shrubs, brushy fields and young woodlands in the northern plains.
spotting_tip: Listen for buzzy songs from the tops of small bushes in grasslands.

fun_fact: Skates lay leathery egg cases, often called mermaid's purses, that wash up on beaches.
where_to_find: Sandy ocean bottoms along the Atlantic coast, sometimes washing up as empty egg cases.
spotting_tip: Look for empty mermaid's purse egg cases in the beach wrack line, and watch the shallows from shore.

fun_fact: Cliff chipmunks live among rocks and can scamper over steep boulders with ease.
where_to_find: Rocky cliffs, canyons and piñon-juniper hillsides.
spotting_tip: Watch rock ledges and boulder piles on sunny mornings for small striped scurrying animals.

fun_fact: Cliff swallows build gourd-shaped mud nests, often in big groups under bridges and cliffs.
where_to_find: Open country near water, with mud nests under bridges, eaves and cliffs.
spotting_tip: Watch bridges and building overhangs for flocks swooping to nests made of mud.

fun_fact: These bright yellow butterflies sometimes migrate in huge numbers.
where_to_find: Sunny gardens, fields, roadsides and sandy open areas.
spotting_tip: Look for fast, bright lemon-yellow butterflies visiting flowers on warm days.

size: 3–4 ft long (90–120 cm), about 2 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Peccaries look like pigs but are a different kind of animal that lives in family herds.
where_to_find: Desert scrub, canyons and brushy areas in the Southwest and Texas.
spotting_tip: Scan brushy washes and desert trails early or late in the day with binoculars.
safety_note: Peccaries can bite and have sharp tusks. Stay back and keep dogs away.

fun_fact: This lizard is an all-female species that lays eggs without needing males.
where_to_find: Rocky and grassy hillsides and washes in western Colorado.
spotting_tip: Look for quick, striped lizards along sunny trails and rocky slopes.

fun_fact: These frogs spend winters under water in cold ponds and streams, resting in the mud.
where_to_find: Cold ponds, marshes and slow streams in mountain valleys.
spotting_tip: Scan pond edges and wet meadows from the bank without disturbing the water.

fun_fact: They hibernate for up to eight months of the year in underground burrows.
where_to_find: Mountain meadows and open grasslands where they dig burrows.
spotting_tip: Look for animals standing up on their hind legs near burrow holes in meadows.

fun_fact: They stack in chains, and the animals at the bottom are mostly female.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, shallow bays and shells in the intertidal zone.
spotting_tip: Look at rocks, shells and tide pools at low tide for stacked, boat-shaped shells.

fun_fact: Large eyespots on its wings can startle birds that try to eat it.
where_to_find: Sunny fields, gardens, roadsides and open, weedy areas.
spotting_tip: Watch bare, sunny ground and flower patches for a brown butterfly with big eyespots.

fun_fact: When scared, a chuckwalla wedges itself into a rock crack and puffs up its body so it cannot be pulled out.
where_to_find: Rocky deserts and lava flows with plenty of boulders.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny boulders in the morning and look for a chunky lizard basking.

fun_fact: Its loud ko-kee call is named for the sound the male frog makes.
where_to_find: Warm, humid forests and gardens with lots of plants.
spotting_tip: Listen for its loud ko-kee call and look for the frog from a path with an adult.

fun_fact: Giant desert centipedes hunt at night and can catch insects and even small lizards.
where_to_find: Dry, rocky areas under logs and stones in deserts and dry grasslands.
spotting_tip: Look from a distance with an adult after dusk, and never flip rocks or logs yourself.
safety_note: Their bite is painful and venomous. Never touch one; use zoom and tell an adult.

fun_fact: Bumble bees buzz their flight muscles to shake pollen loose from flowers.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows, parks and flower-filled fields across the East.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers like clover and bee balm on warm days from a few feet away.
safety_note: Bumble bees can sting if bothered. Stay calm and give them space.

fun_fact: Eider down is among the warmest natural insulation, because the females line their nests with their own feathers.
where_to_find: Rocky coasts and ocean waters along the northeastern shore.
spotting_tip: Scan rocky shores and coastal waters from the shore with binoculars.

fun_fact: Geckos have special toe pads that let them walk up walls and across ceilings.
where_to_find: Houses, porches and walls near lights where insects gather.
spotting_tip: Look near outdoor lights at dusk, where geckos wait for insects.

fun_fact: Chicks can swim and run soon after hatching, and older chicks help care for their siblings.
where_to_find: Freshwater marshes, ponds and lake edges with thick plants.
spotting_tip: Scan the edges of reeds and ponds for a dark bird with a red-and-yellow bill.

fun_fact: It looks like a chipmunk, but it is larger and has no stripes on its face.
where_to_find: Mountain meadows, forest edges and rocky trails.
spotting_tip: Look for round-bodied squirrels with golden heads near picnic areas and trail rocks.

fun_fact: Goldeneyes dive underwater for food and their wings make a whistling sound in flight.
where_to_find: Lakes, rivers and coastal bays, often near forests in the north.
spotting_tip: Scan open water for ducks that dive often, and look for the white spot on a male's cheek.

fun_fact: Their feathers shine with purple, bronze and green in bright sunlight.
where_to_find: Lawns, parks, fields and marshes across the East and Midwest.
spotting_tip: Look on lawns and in parking lots for dark, long-tailed birds with glossy heads.

fun_fact: Loons can dive deep underwater and their wailing calls echo across northern lakes.
where_to_find: Clear northern lakes with forested shores.
spotting_tip: Scan open lake water and listen for haunting wails around dawn and dusk.

fun_fact: Mergansers have thin, toothed bills for catching slippery fish.
where_to_find: Rivers, lakes and reservoirs, especially those with clear water.
spotting_tip: Scan rivers and lakes for long, sleek ducks diving after fish.

fun_fact: Murre chicks leap from cliffs to the sea before they can fly.
where_to_find: Rocky sea cliffs and ocean waters along the coast.
spotting_tip: Look at crowded cliff ledges and nearby ocean water with binoculars.

fun_fact: Mynas are great mimics and can copy many different sounds.
where_to_find: Cities, parks, parking lots and farmland.
spotting_tip: Look for brown birds with yellow eye patches strutting across lawns.

fun_fact: Periwinkles scrape algae off rocks with a tongue-like ribbon covered in tiny teeth.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools along the northeastern coast.
spotting_tip: Check the rocks at low tide for small dark snails clinging to the surface.

fun_fact: Pill woodlice can roll into a tight ball when scared; they are crustaceans, related to crabs.
where_to_find: Gardens, leaf litter and damp places under logs or stones.
spotting_tip: Look near the damp edges of gardens and forest paths with an adult.

fun_fact: This slender snake is a quick swimmer and eats frogs and small fish.
where_to_find: Streams, ponds, marshes and wet meadows.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny banks and shallows along ponds and streams from a distance.

fun_fact: These small butterflies fly in a slow, bouncing way close to the ground.
where_to_find: Grassy fields, meadows and open woodland edges.
spotting_tip: Watch grass tops in sunny meadows for pale, buff-colored butterflies.

fun_fact: Woodlice breathe through gill-like structures, so they need to live in damp places.
where_to_find: Gardens, leaf litter, compost and damp spots under logs and stones.
spotting_tip: Look at damp edges of gardens with an adult and don't pull up large stones.

fun_fact: Males flash bright blue patches on their bellies when they display.
where_to_find: Sagebrush flats, rocky slopes and dry open woodlands.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny rocks and fence posts and watch for small lizards doing push-ups.

fun_fact: A sea star can slowly regrow a lost arm.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, tide pools and shallow ocean waters.
spotting_tip: Peek into tide pools at low tide from the edge and leave sea stars in the water.

fun_fact: Males grow tiny bumps on their heads in spring and turn pink or red.
where_to_find: Clear streams, creeks and small rivers with gravel bottoms.
spotting_tip: Watch quiet pools in clear streams from the bank for small shimmering fish.

fun_fact: Unlike pill woodlice, shiny woodlice cannot roll into a ball.
where_to_find: Gardens, forests and damp places with leaf litter and dead wood.
spotting_tip: Look near damp garden edges with an adult and leave logs and stones in place.

fun_fact: Whiptails are very fast runners that dash between bushes.
where_to_find: Dry grasslands, brush and sandy desert areas.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny sandy ground and watch for striped, speedy lizards.

fun_fact: This woodlouse has a pale stripe down its back and is a quick runner.
where_to_find: Damp gardens, woods and leaf litter.
spotting_tip: Look near damp garden edges with an adult and don't pull up large stones.

fun_fact: Terns hover and then plunge headfirst into the water to catch small fish.
where_to_find: Beaches, bays and coastal islands in summer.
spotting_tip: Watch the water from shore for slender white birds diving for fish.

fun_fact: This lizard is a skilled climber that scurries up walls and rock piles.
where_to_find: Rock walls, railroad embankments and sunny stony areas.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny stone walls and rock piles for small lizards basking in the sun.

fun_fact: Waxbills live in flocks and have a bill the color of red sealing wax.
where_to_find: Grassy fields, gardens and roadsides with seeding grasses.
spotting_tip: Look for tiny brown birds with red bills feeding in small flocks.

fun_fact: Males have a white, powdery covering on the abdomen that develops as they mature.
where_to_find: Ponds, slow streams and wet meadows.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny pond edges and perches for dragonflies patrolling the shoreline.

fun_fact: Males wear a black mask like a tiny bandit.
where_to_find: Marshes, wet meadows and tangly, grassy fields.
spotting_tip: Listen for a rolling wichity-wichity song in the thick brush near water.

size: 14–20 in long (35–50 cm), wingspan 24–35 in (62–90 cm)
fun_fact: This hawk weaves quickly through trees to catch birds in flight.
where_to_find: Forests, suburbs and backyards, sometimes near bird feeders.
spotting_tip: Watch for a long-tailed hawk perched or flying fast near feeders.

fun_fact: Males have a bright purple crown and throat and dive to impress females.
where_to_find: Desert washes, gardens and flowering shrubs.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers like ocotillo and chuparosa, and feeders, for tiny buzzing birds.

fun_fact: They stay buried underground for most of the year and emerge when heavy rain arrives.
where_to_find: Desert grasslands, scrub and temporary rain pools.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud calls after summer storms, but stay on trails and watch from a distance.

size: 16–24 in long, plus 12–16 in tail (40–60 cm + 30–40 cm)
fun_fact: Coypu, also called nutria, have bright orange front teeth and webbed back feet.
where_to_find: Marshes, ponds and slow rivers with plenty of plants.
spotting_tip: Scan marshy shores from a distance around dusk.
safety_note: They can bite if cornered. Keep your distance and keep pets away.

fun_fact: Males build nests by moving small stones into a pile in the stream bed.
where_to_find: Clear creeks and small rivers with gravel and pools.
spotting_tip: Look into creek pools from the bank and wait quietly for fish to appear.

fun_fact: Look for the white cross on its back; it spins a new web almost every day.
where_to_find: Gardens, fences, bushes and the edges of forests.
spotting_tip: Look for round webs shining with morning dew and admire them from a distance.

fun_fact: This is the biggest tree frog in North America, and it has sticky toe pads.
where_to_find: Gardens, porches and wet areas near lights.
spotting_tip: Look for frogs on windows and walls near outdoor lights, and wash your hands after being outside.

fun_fact: It uses its curved bill to dig through dirt for insects.
where_to_find: Desert scrub, cactus gardens and dry yards.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud whit-wheet calls and look for birds perched on cacti.

fun_fact: Juncos flash white outer tail feathers when they fly away.
where_to_find: Forests, yards, parks and feeders across the continent.
spotting_tip: Look for small gray birds hopping on the ground under feeders in winter.

fun_fact: These tiny skinks are fast runners and have shiny, smooth scales.
where_to_find: Gardens, parks and sunny walls with leaf litter.
spotting_tip: Watch sunny patios, rocks and walls for tiny shiny lizards.

fun_fact: The day octopus can change color and texture in a flash to blend with coral.
where_to_find: Shallow coral reefs and rocky seabeds.
spotting_tip: Peek into tide pools from the shore, or snorkel with an adult, looking from a distance.
safety_note: Octopuses can bite. Look but never touch, and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Freshwater mussels clean the water by filtering it as they feed.
where_to_find: Rivers with sandy or gravelly bottoms.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells on riverbanks and leave them where you find them.

fun_fact: This small snake is harmless to people and eats slugs and snails.
where_to_find: Gardens, woodland edges, vacant lots and city parks.
spotting_tip: Watch the edges of gardens and leaf litter from a distance and let the snake go on its way.

size: Body 3–4 in long (8–10 cm), leg span up to 5 in (13 cm)
fun_fact: Tarantulas can regrow lost legs when they molt.
where_to_find: Desert scrub and grasslands, in burrows.
spotting_tip: Look from a distance with an adult after dark and use a flashlight.
safety_note: Tarantulas can bite and flick itchy hairs. Never touch one; use zoom.

fun_fact: Collared lizards can run on two legs when sprinting.
where_to_find: Rocky desert hillsides and canyons.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny boulders and rocky slopes from a distance.

fun_fact: Horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes to scare off coyotes and foxes.
where_to_find: Sandy desert flats and scrublands.
spotting_tip: Scan the ground by trails in morning sun; they are well camouflaged.

fun_fact: Millipedes have many legs and curl into a coil when scared.
where_to_find: Desert scrub, leaf litter and spots under rocks after rain.
spotting_tip: Look at the ground after summer rains and watch without touching.

fun_fact: This nonvenomous snake is often mistaken for a water moccasin.
where_to_find: Swamps, bayous, ponds and slow streams.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and banks from the shore and keep your distance.
safety_note: It can bite if handled. Stay back and use zoom.

fun_fact: Dickcissels sing from fence posts and weeds, and their song sounds like its name.
where_to_find: Prairies, hayfields and weedy meadows.
spotting_tip: Look for a yellow-chested bird singing from a fence post.

fun_fact: Look for the black chevron marks on the back legs.
where_to_find: Weedy fields, roadsides and crop edges.
spotting_tip: Walk through weedy grass on sunny days and watch for leaping insects.

fun_fact: These small snails live on rocks above the water line and can survive out of the water between waves.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and mangroves.
spotting_tip: Look at splash-zone rocks at low tide for small, speckled snails.

fun_fact: After diving, cormorants spread their wings to dry because their feathers soak up water.
where_to_find: Lakes, rivers, bays and coastal waters.
spotting_tip: Watch docks, pilings and branches for dark birds drying their wings.

fun_fact: They store food in burrows and hibernate in winter.
where_to_find: Grasslands, oak woodlands and rocky hills.
spotting_tip: Scan open hillsides and rocky areas for animals sitting beside burrows.

fun_fact: Douglas's squirrels chatter loudly to scold intruders and hide cones for winter.
where_to_find: Evergreen forests.
spotting_tip: Listen for chattering in the treetops and look for cone scraps below.

fun_fact: The downy is North America's smallest woodpecker.
where_to_find: Woodlands, parks, orchards and backyards.
spotting_tip: Watch suet feeders and tree trunks for small black-and-white birds.

fun_fact: A crab sheds its shell to grow larger.
where_to_find: Sandy bottoms and bays along the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools and shallow bays from the shore and enjoy crabs without touching them.

fun_fact: Dunlins fly in tight, twisting flocks that look like swirling clouds.
where_to_find: Beaches, mudflats and coastal marshes.
spotting_tip: Scan mudflats at low tide for flocks probing in the mud.

fun_fact: Dunn's salamander lives beside cold, rocky streams and waterfalls.
where_to_find: Mossy forest streams and seeps.
spotting_tip: Look on wet rainy days along forest streams, from the trail.

fun_fact: Males puff up and make deep hooting sounds in spring.
where_to_find: Mountain forests and brushy slopes.
spotting_tip: Walk quietly along forest-meadow edges and listen for low hoots.

fun_fact: Surgeonfish have tiny, sharp spines near their tails, like little scalpels.
where_to_find: Shallow coral reefs and rocky shores.
spotting_tip: Snorkel with an adult and look at reefs from above.

fun_fact: It is among the smallest dragonflies and waves its abdomen up and down.
where_to_find: Ponds, lake edges and slow streams.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny pond-edge plants for a tiny amber dragonfly.

fun_fact: Small and speedy, they live in cool streams.
where_to_find: Small cold streams and creeks.
spotting_tip: Look for small, darting fish in riffles from the bank.

fun_fact: They sometimes gather in large groups on warm walls in fall.
where_to_find: Around boxelder trees and sunny walls.
spotting_tip: Look for black-and-red bugs on sunny house walls in fall.

fun_fact: This tiny hover fly mimics a bee but cannot sting.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows and flowers.
spotting_tip: Look closely at flower heads on sunny days for tiny hovering flies.

fun_fact: These bees chew round holes in wood to make their nests.
where_to_find: Gardens, wooded edges and wooden structures.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers and wooden porches for large bumble-like bees with shiny abdomens.
safety_note: Carpenter bees can sting. Watch from a distance.

fun_fact: Collared lizards can sprint on their hind legs.
where_to_find: Rocky glades, canyons and open hills.
spotting_tip: Scan boulders in sun from a distance.

fun_fact: Copperheads are well camouflaged in leaves and have hourglass-shaped bands.
where_to_find: Wooded hillsides, rocky areas and forest edges.
active_time: Dusk and night in summer, daytime in spring and fall
spotting_tip: Stay on trails and scan the ground ahead; never step over logs without looking.
safety_note: Copperheads are venomous. Never touch or try to move one; step back and tell an adult.

fun_fact: This damselfly holds its wings along its body when resting.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and slow streams.
spotting_tip: Watch pond-edge plants for a tiny blue-and-black damselfly.

fun_fact: When scared, it shakes its tail in dry leaves and sounds like a rattlesnake, but it is harmless.
where_to_find: Prairies, farm fields and wetland edges.
spotting_tip: Look from a distance along trails and fields.
safety_note: Do not handle it. It can bite if frightened, so use zoom.

fun_fact: Kingbirds fiercely chase away hawks and crows.
where_to_find: Open fields, fence lines and shorelines.
spotting_tip: Look for birds with white-tipped tails perched on fences.

fun_fact: Voles make little runways in the grass.
where_to_find: Grassy fields and meadows.
spotting_tip: Look at the grass for small tunnels in the thick growth.

fun_fact: Though often mistaken for a copperhead, it is harmless and eats mice.
where_to_find: Farms, forest edges and rocky hillsides.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny paths from a distance.
safety_note: It may bite if frightened. Do not handle it.

fun_fact: Moles tunnel underground, leaving ridges across lawns.
where_to_find: Lawns, fields and loose soil.
spotting_tip: Look for raised tunnel ridges in yards and fields.

fun_fact: These tiny fish eat mosquito larvae.
where_to_find: Ponds, ditches and slow, shallow water.
spotting_tip: Look in shallow pond edges for tiny fish near the surface.

fun_fact: This small turtle can close its shell with hinges.
where_to_find: Ponds, ditches and marshes.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and banks from a distance.

fun_fact: Also called a stinkpot, it gives off a smelly musk when scared.
where_to_find: Ponds, slow streams and marshes.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank for small turtles on logs and in the shallows.

fun_fact: Its call sounds like a buzzing sheep.
where_to_find: Moist woods, leaf litter and temporary pools.
spotting_tip: Listen for buzzing after rain and view from the trail.

fun_fact: Phoebes wag their tails when perched.
where_to_find: Woodland edges, bridges and porches.
spotting_tip: Look for a bird wagging its tail on low perches near water.

fun_fact: Female pondhawks are bright green while males turn blue.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and garden edges.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny pond edges for green or blue dragonflies.

fun_fact: Ratsnakes are excellent climbers that help control rodents.
where_to_find: Woodlands, farms and rocky areas.
spotting_tip: Look from a distance on logs and trees.
safety_note: Ratsnakes can bite if scared. Do not handle one.

fun_fact: These salamanders have no lungs and breathe through their skin.
where_to_find: Moist forest floors under leaves and logs.
spotting_tip: Watch damp forest floors from the trail and leave logs in place.

size: 4–5 in long (10–13 cm), wingspan 11–13 in (28–33 cm)
fun_fact: Red bats roost in trees where they look like dead leaves.
where_to_find: Wooded areas, tree lines and parks.
spotting_tip: Watch the evening sky near trees with an adult.
safety_note: Never touch a bat, even one on the ground. Bats can carry rabies. Tell an adult.

fun_fact: Spadefoots dig backward into sandy soil with a special spade on each hind foot.
where_to_find: Sandy soils, woods and rain pools.
spotting_tip: Listen for calls after heavy rain, and watch from the trail.

fun_fact: A tiny butterfly with little tails on its hind wings.
where_to_find: Meadows, fields and gardens.
spotting_tip: Watch clover patches for tiny blue butterflies.

fun_fact: Their caterpillars build silk tents in tree branches.
where_to_find: Orchards, forest edges and wild cherry trees.
spotting_tip: Look for silky tents in branches in spring, from a distance.

fun_fact: Tiger salamanders spend much of the year in underground burrows.
where_to_find: Ponds, wooded areas and prairies.
spotting_tip: Watch for them on rainy nights near ponds, from the trail, with an adult.

fun_fact: Towhees scratch the ground with both feet to find food under leaves.
where_to_find: Brushy woods, forest edges and thickets.
spotting_tip: Listen for drink-your-tea calls and look under brush.

fun_fact: Its black wings and metallic green body shimmer in sunlight.
where_to_find: Shaded streams and woodland creeks.
spotting_tip: Look along shady stream edges for shimmering damselflies.

fun_fact: Caterpillars feed on desert hackberry leaves.
where_to_find: Desert streams and woodlands with hackberry trees.
spotting_tip: Look for butterflies perched on trees near streams.

fun_fact: This dove spread across North America within a few decades.
where_to_find: Towns, farms and backyards.
spotting_tip: Look for large pale doves on wires, rooftops and feeders.

fun_fact: Carp can live for many years and grow quite large.
where_to_find: Lakes, ponds, rivers and canals.
spotting_tip: Watch shallow water from banks and bridges for large fish near the surface.

fun_fact: Firebugs often gather in big red-and-black groups, and their bold colors warn predators that they taste bad.
where_to_find: Sunny spots near linden trees, mallow plants and warm building walls.
spotting_tip: Look for red-and-black clusters at the base of trees on warm days.

fun_fact: Despite the name, green crabs can also be brown, orange or even reddish.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, tide pools and salt marshes along the Northeast coast.
spotting_tip: Look into tide pools from the edge at low tide and watch for sideways scuttling.
safety_note: Crabs can pinch. Watch from the edge of the tide pool and don't pick them up.

fun_fact: Mantises can turn their heads to look over their shoulders, which almost no other insect can do.
where_to_find: Sunny meadows, gardens and tall grass in the Northwest and Mountain West.
spotting_tip: Scan tall grass and flower stems slowly; mantises stay very still.

fun_fact: Paper wasps make their nests from chewed wood fibers mixed with saliva, which dries into paper.
where_to_find: Under eaves, on fences and in garden shrubs near homes.
spotting_tip: Spot the small paper nest from far away with your zoom.
safety_note: Wasps can sting. Stay away from nests and use zoom.

fun_fact: Starlings can copy the sounds of other birds and even things like car alarms and phone rings.
where_to_find: Lawns, farms, parks and city streets across much of the country.
spotting_tip: Look for shiny dark birds walking on lawns; in winter they are covered in white speckles.

fun_fact: Its caterpillars spin big silky tents over the ends of tree branches and eat leaves safely inside.
where_to_find: Woodlands, yards and roadsides with hardwood trees.
spotting_tip: Look for white silk webs on branch tips in late summer, and pale moths resting nearby.

fun_fact: Male fantail darters guard the eggs that are stuck to the underside of flat rocks.
where_to_find: Clear, rocky creeks and streams.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow, clear riffles from the bank; polarized sunglasses help.

fun_fact: In spring, male fathead minnows grow bumps on their snouts and turn dark while they guard their nests.
where_to_find: Ponds, slow creeks and prairie wetlands.
spotting_tip: Watch the shallow edges of ponds from the bank for small schools of fish.

fun_fact: A female fatmucket waves a flap of skin shaped like a little fish to lure real fish close, so her baby mussels can hitch a ride.
where_to_find: Sandy or gravelly bottoms of streams, rivers and lakes.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells along the bank and in clear shallows, and leave them where they are.

fun_fact: Skippers get their name from their quick, darting flight that looks like skipping.
where_to_find: Lawns, parks and flower gardens.
spotting_tip: Watch flower beds and lawns on sunny afternoons for small orange butterflies.

fun_fact: Despite the name, fishers rarely eat fish; they are one of the few animals that hunt porcupines.
where_to_find: Dense northern forests.
spotting_tip: Fishers are shy and rarely seen; look for tracks in snow near forest trails.
safety_note: Fishers can bite and scratch. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Florida bass can grow bigger than most other largemouth bass.
where_to_find: Weedy lakes, ponds and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Watch near lily pads and fallen trees at the water's edge from the shore.

fun_fact: When scared, a cottonmouth opens its mouth wide to show the pale, cotton-white lining inside.
where_to_find: Swamps, marshes, ponds and slow streams.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and banks near water from a safe distance; never reach into the water or brush.
safety_note: Cottonmouths are venomous. Never touch or approach one; use zoom and step away slowly.

fun_fact: Gars can gulp air at the surface, which helps them live in warm water with little oxygen.
where_to_find: Warm, weedy lakes, canals and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Look from bridges and docks for long, thin fish floating still near the surface.

fun_fact: Young cooters eat lots of insects, but adults mostly eat water plants.
where_to_find: Lakes, ponds and slow rivers with plants.
spotting_tip: Look for turtles basking on logs in the morning sun.

fun_fact: Its shell is leathery instead of hard, and its long snout works like a snorkel.
where_to_find: Lakes, canals and slow rivers with sandy bottoms.
spotting_tip: Look for flat, pancake-shaped turtles resting on banks and sandbars from a distance.
safety_note: Softshell turtles have long necks and can bite. Watch from far away.

fun_fact: Forster's terns dive headfirst into the water to catch small fish.
where_to_find: Coastal marshes, bays and beaches.
spotting_tip: Watch for white birds hovering over the water and then plunging in.

fun_fact: Its call sounds like a nasal, buzzing 'waaah' that can carry across a whole pond.
where_to_find: Sandy soils near ponds, floodplains and dunes.
spotting_tip: Listen for the call near ponds on warm spring evenings, then look with an adult along the shore.

fun_fact: Damselflies fold their wings along their body when they rest, which dragonflies can't do.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and slow streams with plants.
spotting_tip: Look on reeds and pond plants near the water on sunny days.

fun_fact: The papershell is named for its shell, which is thin and light like paper.
where_to_find: Muddy or sandy bottoms of big rivers and lakes.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells along the riverbank, and leave them where they lie.

fun_fact: Franklin's ground squirrels hibernate underground for most of the year, from fall until spring.
where_to_find: Tall-grass prairies and brushy field edges.
spotting_tip: Watch for squirrels popping up from burrows in tall grass; stay quiet and still.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite and carry germs. Never feed or touch them.

fun_fact: This squirrel stashes pine cones in big piles to eat during the winter.
where_to_find: Pine and fir forests in the mountains.
spotting_tip: Listen for chattering and look for piles of cone scales under conifers.

fun_fact: Dogwinkles drill tiny holes through barnacle and mussel shells to eat what's inside.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools in cool Pacific waters.
spotting_tip: Look on rocks near barnacles in tide pools, and don't pry them off.

fun_fact: Bumble bees can shake flowers loose with their flight muscles to knock out pollen, called buzz pollination.
where_to_find: Mountain meadows, gardens and forest edges.
spotting_tip: Watch flower patches on sunny days for fuzzy, bumbling bees.
safety_note: Bees sting only if bothered. Use zoom and give them space.

fun_fact: Gadwalls look plain gray-brown, but males have a bold black tail end and a white patch on the wing.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and lakes with plants.
spotting_tip: Look for ducks tipping tail-up to eat water plants from the bottom.

fun_fact: Quail chicks can run and feed themselves just hours after hatching.
where_to_find: Desert scrub, dry washes and suburban yards.
spotting_tip: Listen for the 'chi-CA-go' call and look for groups scurrying in a line under bushes.

fun_fact: A garden snail's tongue is covered in thousands of tiny teeth.
where_to_find: Gardens, damp yards and shady walls.
spotting_tip: Look on leaves and walls on damp mornings or after rain.

fun_fact: Its front legs are shaped like fangs that deliver venom to catch crickets, lizards and even mice.
where_to_find: Dry, rocky deserts and canyons.
spotting_tip: Rarely seen; if you spot one on a trail, use zoom and let it pass.
safety_note: The bite is painful and venomous. Never touch it and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Giant floaters live in muddy ponds where many mussels can't, and their babies hitch rides on fish.
where_to_find: Muddy ponds, lakes and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells along the shoreline, and leave them where they are.

fun_fact: Giant house spiders spin funnel-shaped webs and wait inside for insects to wander by.
where_to_find: Dark corners of sheds, garages, basements and woodpiles.
spotting_tip: Look for flat, funnel-shaped webs in corners, and watch from a distance.
safety_note: Spiders can bite if squeezed. Use zoom and let it be.

fun_fact: Gila woodpeckers carve nest holes into saguaro cactus, and the cactus grows a hard wall around the hole.
where_to_find: Saguaro desert, wooded washes and desert yards.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud rolling calls and look for round holes in saguaros.

fun_fact: This is one of the biggest gulls, and its wingtips are pale instead of black.
where_to_find: Arctic coasts, harbors and shorelines.
spotting_tip: Look for big, pale gulls among other gulls at harbors and beaches.

fun_fact: These gulls drop shellfish onto rocks or pavement to crack them open.
where_to_find: Coasts, harbors, docks and town parking lots.
spotting_tip: Look for gulls with gray wingtips instead of black along the shore.

fun_fact: Day geckos have no eyelids, so they lick their eyes clean.
where_to_find: Palm trees, banana plants, fences and gardens in warm lowlands.
spotting_tip: Scan trunks and leaves slowly for bright green geckos with gold flecks.

fun_fact: Crayfish can shoot backward in a flash by flipping their tails.
where_to_find: Rocky streams and rivers.
spotting_tip: Look into clear, shallow water from the bank.
safety_note: Crayfish can pinch. Watch from the bank with an adult.

fun_fact: Its song sounds like a sad 'oh dear me', so some people call it 'Weary Willie'.
where_to_find: Brushy thickets, gardens and forest edges in winter.
spotting_tip: Look for a yellow stripe on the head among bushes near seeds and berries.

size: Leg span 3–4 in (7.5–10 cm), females much larger than males
fun_fact: The silk of this spider shines golden in the sun and is very strong.
where_to_find: Woodland edges, gardens and trails with big webs between trees.
spotting_tip: Look for big webs with a golden shine between trees, and stay a few steps back.
safety_note: Its bite is rare and mild, but never touch the spider or its web.

fun_fact: Soldier beetles are nicknamed leatherwings, and they visit goldenrod flowers in late summer.
where_to_find: Meadows and roadsides with goldenrod.
spotting_tip: Check goldenrod flowers in late summer for slim orange-and-black beetles.

fun_fact: Its big, golden eyes give it its name, and it likes to leap for insects at the surface.
where_to_find: Muddy big rivers and lakes.
spotting_tip: Watch the surface from a dock or bank for small rings from rising fish.

fun_fact: Gopher tortoises dig burrows up to 40 ft long that hundreds of other animals share.
where_to_find: Dry, sandy pinelands, dunes and scrub.
spotting_tip: Look for half-moon burrow entrances with sandy mounds, and watch quietly from far away.

fun_fact: Catbirds make a cat-like 'meow' and also copy other birds' songs.
where_to_find: Dense thickets, hedges and forest edges.
spotting_tip: Listen for a cat-like mew from shrubs and look for a slim gray bird with a dark cap.

fun_fact: It rubs its back wings together so the little 'tail' looks like a head, which fools predators.
where_to_find: Weedy fields, gardens and roadsides.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers in sunny spots for small gray butterflies with tiny tails.

fun_fact: Sea stars have no brain, and tiny tube feet under each arm help them crawl.
where_to_find: Sandy shallow sea bottoms and beaches in warm water.
spotting_tip: Look in clear shallow water at low tide, and never take one out of the water.

fun_fact: Gray snappers are also called mangrove snappers because the young grow up among mangrove roots.
where_to_find: Mangroves, reefs and docks in warm coastal waters.
spotting_tip: Look for schools around piers and mangrove roots in clear water.

fun_fact: Gray treefrogs can change color between gray and green to match tree bark.
where_to_find: Trees and shrubs near woodland ponds and in yards.
spotting_tip: Listen for a trill on warm evenings and look with an adult near ponds.

fun_fact: Wolves howl to keep their pack in touch, and the sound can carry for miles.
where_to_find: Forests, mountain valleys and open meadows.
spotting_tip: Scan valleys at dawn with binoculars from road pullouts.
safety_note: Stay in the car or far back. Never approach or feed wild wolves.

fun_fact: Spadefoots spend most of the year buried underground and come out after heavy rains.
where_to_find: Sagebrush flats, dry grasslands and temporary pools.
spotting_tip: Rarely seen; after spring rains, listen near temporary pools with an adult.

fun_fact: This is the largest gull in the world.
where_to_find: Coasts, harbors, beaches and landfills.
spotting_tip: Look for the biggest gull in a flock, with a black back and pink legs.

size: 33–41 in long (85–105 cm), wingspan 7–8 ft (2.1–2.4 m)
fun_fact: Males puff up a huge red throat pouch to attract mates, and they steal food from other seabirds in flight.
where_to_find: Open ocean and rocky coasts and islands.
spotting_tip: Look up for a black bird with a forked tail soaring high without flapping.

fun_fact: Female skinks guard their eggs and keep them moist until they hatch.
where_to_find: Rocky grasslands, canyons and prairie hillsides.
spotting_tip: Look near rock edges on sunny mornings, and watch quietly from a distance.

fun_fact: The Great Plains toad's trill sounds like a small jackhammer.
where_to_find: Prairies, deserts and farm fields near temporary pools.
spotting_tip: Listen for trills after rain, and look near puddles with an adult.

fun_fact: The silver spots on the underside of its wings look like shiny coins.
where_to_find: Meadows, open woods and flowery roadsides.
spotting_tip: Look for large orange butterflies on thistles and milkweed.

fun_fact: Males have a very long tail and make loud whistles, clicks and squeaks.
where_to_find: Parking lots, farms, marsh edges and city parks.
spotting_tip: Look for glossy black birds with long tails strutting in lots and lawns.

fun_fact: It curls its tail to show a black-and-white underside as a signal and sprints with the tail held high.
where_to_find: Rocky deserts and canyons.
spotting_tip: Look on sunny rocks and gravel, and watch quietly from a distance.

fun_fact: Unlike most lizards, this horned lizard gives birth to live babies.
where_to_find: Sagebrush, grasslands and open pine areas.
spotting_tip: Look carefully at bare ground near ant mounds; they blend in well.

fun_fact: Its loud 'whew-whew-whew' alarm call warns other birds that danger is near.
where_to_find: Mudflats, marshes and pond edges.
spotting_tip: Look for tall shorebirds with long yellow legs wading in shallow water.

fun_fact: In the wild, these frogs get their skin toxins from the tiny ants and mites they eat.
where_to_find: Damp forest floors and rock walls near streams.
spotting_tip: Look on mossy rocks and leaf litter in humid forests, using zoom.
safety_note: The skin can be toxic. Never touch it; use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Green herons drop bait like bread, feathers or insects onto the water to lure fish, which is real tool use.
where_to_find: Wooded ponds, marsh edges and streams.
spotting_tip: Look for a hunched dark bird crouching on a branch or log over the water.

fun_fact: Iguanas have a 'third eye' on top of the head that senses light and shadows.
where_to_find: Trees along canals, parks and waterfronts.
spotting_tip: Look up in trees and along canal banks where iguanas bask in the sun.
safety_note: Iguanas can bite and whip their tails. Watch from far away.

fun_fact: Unlike most sea turtles, adults eat mostly seagrass and algae.
where_to_find: Warm coastal waters, seagrass beds and reefs, and some Hawaii beaches.
spotting_tip: Look from the beach or shore in clear water, and keep far back.
safety_note: These turtles are protected by law. Watch quietly and never touch or chase them.

fun_fact: Males dig a shallow dish-shaped nest and guard the eggs.
where_to_find: Ponds, creeks and small lakes with weeds.
spotting_tip: Look near weeds and logs in shallow water from the bank.

fun_fact: It is the smallest dabbling duck in North America.
where_to_find: Shallow ponds, marshes and mudflats.
spotting_tip: Look for small ducks with a bold green patch behind the eye.

fun_fact: These frogs skip the tadpole stage; tiny frogs hatch right out of eggs laid on land.
where_to_find: Leaf litter, gardens and flowerpots.
spotting_tip: Listen for soft chirps in gardens in the evening and look with an adult.

fun_fact: Millipedes have two pairs of legs on most body segments.
where_to_find: Compost piles, flowerpots and damp mulch.
spotting_tip: Look at damp soil and mulch near flower beds after rain, from a distance.

fun_fact: In spring, males show off bright green bars and orange on their fins.
where_to_find: Fast, rocky riffles in clear streams.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow, rocky riffles from the bank in spring.

fun_fact: Grey francolins would rather run than fly, and males call loudly at dawn.
where_to_find: Dry grasslands, pastures and roadsides.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud calls and watch roadside grass edges.

fun_fact: Grey seals are nicknamed horsehead seals for their long, sloping noses.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, sandy islands and offshore ledges.
spotting_tip: Look for resting seals on distant sandbars, or join a seal-watching boat tour.
safety_note: Seals are wild and can bite. Use zoom, stay far back and never approach.

fun_fact: Buck moths fly in the daytime, unlike most big moths.
where_to_find: Sunny oak woods and edges.
spotting_tip: Look for black-and-white moths flying in sunny oak woods; never touch the spiny caterpillars.
safety_note: Buck moth caterpillars have spines that sting. Never touch them.

fun_fact: Gulf Coast toads gather at puddles and ponds after heavy rain to sing and breed.
where_to_find: Lawns, ditches and marsh edges.
spotting_tip: Look with an adult at dusk near porch lights where toads wait for insects.

fun_fact: Males have a bright orange belly and a long ear flap.
where_to_find: Clear creeks with sand and gravel.
spotting_tip: Look into slow, clear pools from the bank.

fun_fact: Prairie dogs greet each other with a kiss and use different barks for different dangers.
where_to_find: High grasslands and mountain meadows.
spotting_tip: Look for burrow mounds with upright sentries standing guard.
safety_note: Prairie dogs can bite and carry fleas. Never feed or touch them.

fun_fact: Hackberry emperors prefer sap and rotting fruit to flower nectar, and may even land on people.
where_to_find: Woods and wooded streams with hackberry trees.
spotting_tip: Look near hackberry trees and shady trails for butterflies resting on tree trunks.

fun_fact: Its tongue is so long that it wraps around the back of its skull.
where_to_find: Mature forests, woodlots and backyard feeders.
spotting_tip: Listen for drumming and look for black-and-white birds climbing tree trunks.

fun_fact: Its orange wings with dark bands look like Halloween colors.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and ditches in sunny spots.
spotting_tip: Look for dragonflies perched on the tips of tall plants near water.

fun_fact: Harbour porpoises are shy and rarely leap, unlike dolphins.
where_to_find: Cool coastal waters and bays.
spotting_tip: Look from ferries or headlands on calm days for a small dark fin rolling at the surface.

fun_fact: Harlequin ducks swim in rushing rapids and crashing ocean surf.
where_to_find: Rushing mountain streams in summer and rocky coasts.
spotting_tip: Look for small, colorful ducks bobbing in fast water near rocks.

fun_fact: Antelope squirrels are active in desert heat and hold their tails over their backs for shade.
where_to_find: Rocky desert slopes and saguaro scrub.
spotting_tip: Look on rocky slopes for small squirrels with a white stripe on each side.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite and carry germs. Never feed or touch them.

fun_fact: This is the largest sparrow in North America, and it nests only in far northern Canada.
where_to_find: Brushy fields, hedgerows and backyard feeders in winter.
spotting_tip: Look for a sparrow with a black bib under hedges and near feeders.

fun_fact: Its curved bill is perfect for sipping nectar from flowers.
where_to_find: Native forests, mountain slopes and some gardens.
spotting_tip: Look for small yellow-green birds visiting flowering trees.

fun_fact: Hawaiian black nerites live on wave-splashed rocks and clamp down tight to stay put.
where_to_find: Rocky, wave-splashed shores.
spotting_tip: Look from safe, dry rocks, and never turn your back on the waves.

fun_fact: Surgeonfish have a sharp spine at the base of the tail, like a tiny scalpel.
where_to_find: Shallow rocky reefs and tide pools.
spotting_tip: Look in clear shallow water for striped fish grazing on algae.

fun_fact: Its white forehead shield stands out, and its lobed toes make it a strong swimmer.
where_to_find: Freshwater ponds, marshes and taro fields.
spotting_tip: Look for dark swimming birds with a white forehead at pond edges.

fun_fact: It weaves a big round web with a bright zigzag stripe in the center.
where_to_find: Gardens, forest edges and shrubs.
spotting_tip: Look for round webs with a zigzag stripe between bushes, from a few steps away.
safety_note: Spiders can bite if bothered. Never touch the spider or its web.

fun_fact: The nene is Hawaii's state bird, and its feet have less webbing than other geese for walking on lava.
where_to_find: Grassy slopes, lava fields and volcano parks.
spotting_tip: Look for brownish-gray geese with a black cap on grassy slopes; never feed them.

fun_fact: It is Hawaii's only native land mammal.
where_to_find: Forests, shrubland and coasts.
spotting_tip: Look at dusk for fast, zigzagging flights over open spaces, and stay with an adult.
safety_note: Never touch a bat; bats can carry rabies. Use zoom.

fun_fact: It is one of the rarest seals in the world and lives only in Hawaii.
where_to_find: Sandy beaches and rocky shores.
spotting_tip: Look on quiet beaches for a resting seal that looks like a big gray log.
safety_note: Monk seals are protected and can bite. Stay far back and never approach.

fun_fact: Cowries have glossy shells because their soft body covers the shell like a coat.
where_to_find: Rocky reefs and tide pools.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide and leave shells where you find them.

fun_fact: Its song sounds like a flute, and it is the state bird of Vermont.
where_to_find: Cool forests and thickets with leaf litter.
spotting_tip: Listen for flute-like song and look for a brown bird with a spotted chest.

fun_fact: The caterpillar is fuzzy white with black tufts, and its bristly hairs can irritate skin.
where_to_find: Woods and yards with hickory, walnut and oak trees.
spotting_tip: Look for fuzzy white caterpillars on leaves in late summer, using zoom.
safety_note: Fuzzy caterpillars can make skin itchy. Look but don't touch.

fun_fact: Stonerollers get their name from moving small stones to build their nests.
where_to_find: Clear, gravelly Ozark streams.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow gravel riffles from the bank.

fun_fact: Baby cotton rats are born furry with their eyes open and can walk soon after.
where_to_find: Grassy fields, weedy roadsides and field edges.
spotting_tip: Look for little runways through thick grass from the path.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite and carry germs. Never feed or touch them.

fun_fact: Hoary marmots give a loud whistle as an alarm, so they are nicknamed whistlers.
where_to_find: Rocky slopes and alpine meadows above the treeline.
spotting_tip: Scan boulder fields at high elevation and listen for whistles.
safety_note: Marmots can bite. Use zoom and never feed them.

fun_fact: Males raise and lower a fan-shaped white crest, and they can see well underwater when hunting fish.
where_to_find: Wooded ponds, rivers and lakes.
spotting_tip: Look for a small duck with a big fan-shaped crest on quiet, wooded water.

fun_fact: Chipmunks carry seeds in stretchy cheek pouches.
where_to_find: Rocky juniper and pinyon slopes.
spotting_tip: Look for striped chipmunks darting over rocks and logs.

fun_fact: It eats stinging animals like hydroids and keeps their stingers for its own defense.
where_to_find: Rocky tide pools and docks on the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide for a colorful sea slug with orange tips.
safety_note: Its body can sting. Look but don't touch.

fun_fact: Puffins can carry several small fish at once in their colorful bills.
where_to_find: Sea cliffs, rocky islands and open ocean.
spotting_tip: Join a boat tour and look for black-and-white birds with orange bills on sea cliffs.

size: 1–1.5 in long body (2.5–4 cm), longer with legs
fun_fact: House centipedes have 15 pairs of legs and eat spiders and roaches.
where_to_find: Damp basements, bathrooms and closets.
spotting_tip: They dash across floors quickly; watch from a distance and let them go.
safety_note: House centipedes rarely bite but can. Let it be.

fun_fact: House sparrows came from Europe and now live near people all over the world.
where_to_find: Cities, farms, yards and outdoor cafes.
spotting_tip: Look for small brown-and-gray birds hopping near sidewalks and feeders.

fun_fact: Each spring, a queen bumble bee starts a brand-new colony all on her own.
where_to_find: Western meadows, prairies and gardens.
spotting_tip: Watch flower patches on sunny days for fuzzy bees with a yellow-and-black body.
safety_note: Bees sting only if bothered. Use zoom and give them space.

fun_fact: Skippers get their name from their quick, darting flight that looks like skipping.
where_to_find: Lawns, fields, gardens and roadsides.
spotting_tip: Look for small orange-brown butterflies zipping between flowers.

fun_fact: Its curved bill fits perfectly into red lobelia flowers, and old Hawaiian featherwork used its feathers.
where_to_find: Native mountain forests with ohia blossoms.
spotting_tip: Look for bright red birds with curved orange bills in flowering ohia trees.

fun_fact: Males aren't blue from pigment; their feathers scatter light to look blue.
where_to_find: Brushy field edges, roadsides and woods edges.
spotting_tip: Look for tiny blue birds singing from high perches in the morning.

fun_fact: It uses its teeth and spines to carve little burrows in rock and hides inside.
where_to_find: Rocky reefs and surf-zone tide pools.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide, and wear shoes at the shore.
safety_note: Spines can hurt. Look but don't touch.

fun_fact: Its fuzzy caterpillar, the woolly bear, can freeze solid in winter and thaw out in spring.
where_to_find: Fields, gardens, forest edges and roadsides.
spotting_tip: Look for fuzzy black-and-orange caterpillars crossing paths in fall.

fun_fact: Its tail can break off to help it escape from predators, and then grow back.
where_to_find: Rock walls, rail embankments and gardens.
spotting_tip: Look on sunny stone walls and rocks and watch quietly.

fun_fact: Males have three horns like a Triceratops, and each eye can look in a different direction.
where_to_find: Shrubs and trees in wet forests and gardens.
spotting_tip: Look for slow-moving green lizards in branches.

fun_fact: Japanese beetles gather in groups on leaves and shine metallic green and copper.
where_to_find: Lawns, gardens and rose bushes.
spotting_tip: Look on leaves and flowers on sunny summer days.

fun_fact: Its big pink bill and white cheek patch make it easy to recognize, and it came originally from Indonesia.
where_to_find: Parks, lawns and grassy edges near towns.
spotting_tip: Look for gray birds with a white cheek and pink bill on lawns.

fun_fact: Johnny darters dart in short hops along the bottom, and males guard eggs under rocks.
where_to_find: Sandy and gravel bottoms in streams and lakes.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow, clear water from the bank for tiny hopping fish.

fun_fact: Jonah crabs have strong claws that can crack open shells.
where_to_find: Rocky, cold ocean bottoms and sometimes tide pools.
spotting_tip: See them in aquariums, or look into tide pools at low tide from the edge.
safety_note: Crabs can pinch hard. Use zoom and don't pick them up.

fun_fact: Males are shiny blue-black with a white crest, and the birds come from the Himalayas.
where_to_find: Mountain forests and forest edges.
spotting_tip: Look for birds walking along forest trails at dawn.

fun_fact: If a predator gets too close to its nest, a killdeer pretends to have a broken wing to lure it away.
where_to_find: Open fields, parking lots, gravel and lawns.
spotting_tip: Listen for a loud 'kill-deer' call and look for two black bands on the chest.

fun_fact: It is named for the black-and-white bars on its back, which look like a ladder.
where_to_find: Desert scrub, mesquite and yucca.
spotting_tip: Listen for tapping on cactus and yucca stalks.

fun_fact: Lake trout can live for decades.
where_to_find: Deep, cold lakes.
spotting_tip: Hard to see in deep water; visit a fish hatchery or a fishing pier with an adult.

fun_fact: Lapland longspurs nest on the Arctic tundra and spend winter in open fields in huge flocks.
where_to_find: Arctic tundra and open fields.
spotting_tip: Scan open fields in winter for flocks that fly up all at once.

size: Fly about 0.1 in (3 mm); gall about 0.5 in (1.3 cm)
fun_fact: The larvae live inside a small fuzzy gall on a creosote bush, which is their own tiny home.
where_to_find: Creosote bush deserts.
spotting_tip: Look for fuzzy lumps on creosote bush branches.

fun_fact: Its hidden yellow-orange hindwings flash in flight and vanish when it lands.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows and fields near edges.
spotting_tip: Check porch lights in the morning for resting moths.

fun_fact: The largemouth bass has such a big mouth that its jaw reaches past its eye.
where_to_find: Weedy lakes, ponds and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Watch near lily pads and fallen trees at the water's edge from the shore.

fun_fact: Stonerollers move small stones to build their nests.
where_to_find: Clear, gravelly creeks.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow gravel riffles from the bank.

fun_fact: Males perform a courtship dance, strutting with fanned tails and drooped wings.
where_to_find: Open grasslands, farm edges and roadsides with fence posts.
spotting_tip: Look for sparrows with a bold face pattern perched on fence posts.

fun_fact: Its call sounds like laughing: 'ha-ha-ha-ha'.
where_to_find: Beaches, harbors and coastal marshes.
spotting_tip: Listen for laughing calls and look for a black head in summer.

size: Wingspan 6.5–7 ft (2–2.1 m), body about 31 in (79 cm)
fun_fact: Albatrosses do elaborate courtship dances and glide over the ocean for hours without flapping.
where_to_find: Open ocean and sandy island nesting colonies.
spotting_tip: Visit a viewing area with fences and use binoculars; never enter the nesting area.

fun_fact: Young males copy songs from their neighbors.
where_to_find: Brushy hillsides and stream thickets.
spotting_tip: Look for bright blue birds singing from bushes in the morning.

fun_fact: Its striped caterpillars were introduced to control the leafy spurge weed.
where_to_find: Fields and rangeland with leafy spurge.
spotting_tip: Look for brightly colored caterpillars on spurge plants from a distance; spurge sap can irritate skin.

fun_fact: The least chipmunk is one of the smallest chipmunks in North America and stuffs its cheeks with seeds to carry home.
where_to_find: Sagebrush, open pine forests and rocky slopes across the Rockies.
spotting_tip: Watch fallen logs and rocky edges in the morning; it darts quickly with its tail held up.

fun_fact: The leather star has smooth, slippery skin and eats other sea creatures, including other sea stars.
where_to_find: Rocky tide pools and shallow, cold coastal waters.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide from the edge; never pull sea stars off rocks.

fun_fact: Lesser goldfinches sing sweet songs and sometimes copy the calls of other birds.
where_to_find: Open woods, weedy fields, backyards and streamsides across the Southwest and West.
spotting_tip: Look for tiny yellow birds on seed heads and at thistle feeders.

fun_fact: Ligated furrow bees nest in tunnels dug in the ground and visit many different flowers.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows, parks and sunny flower patches.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers on warm mornings for small, shiny, metallic-looking bees.
safety_note: Bees can sting if bothered. Use zoom and let them be.

fun_fact: Limpkins eat apple snails and have a loud, wailing call that sounds like screaming.
where_to_find: Freshwater marshes, swamps and shady riverbanks.
spotting_tip: Scan shallow marsh edges for a brown, white-speckled bird probing for snails.

fun_fact: A chiton wears eight armor plates like a tiny knight and clings tightly to rocks with its foot.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools along the cold Pacific coast.
active_time: Night, but visible at low tide
spotting_tip: Look at low tide for pink-lined oval shells stuck to rocks; do not pull them off.

size: 22–29 in long (56–74 cm), wingspan about 40 in (102 cm)
fun_fact: Little blue herons are born white and slowly turn slate blue as they grow up.
where_to_find: Marshes, ponds, swamps and coastal shallows across the South.
spotting_tip: Look for a slow, quiet wader along shallow water edges.

fun_fact: If a predator grabs its tail, this skink can drop the tail and wiggle away to escape.
where_to_find: Leaf litter in forests, yards and gardens in the Southeast.
spotting_tip: Watch quietly beside leaf piles in sunny spots for a flicker of shiny brown.

fun_fact: Hermit crabs borrow empty snail shells and move to a bigger one as they grow.
where_to_find: Sandy and muddy shallows, tide pools and coastal waters on the Atlantic coast.
spotting_tip: Look in shallow tide pools for a moving snail shell; look but leave it in place.

fun_fact: This speedy lizard can run on just its back legs, and its spots help it blend in with desert gravel.
where_to_find: Sagebrush flats and dry open desert basins in the West.
spotting_tip: Scan open, sandy patches from a distance with zoom on warm mornings.

fun_fact: Long-toed salamanders live in cold mountains and head to breeding ponds just as the snow melts.
where_to_find: Forests, meadows and mountain ponds in the Northwest.
spotting_tip: After rain, look near ponds from the trail edge; never flip logs or rocks.

fun_fact: Male longear sunfish are among the most colorful fish in streams, with bright orange bellies and blue stripes.
where_to_find: Clear streams, creeks and rivers with gravel bottoms.
spotting_tip: Look from a bridge or bank on clear water; sunglasses help cut the glare.

fun_fact: Longfin dace are tiny desert fish that can survive in very warm, low-oxygen water.
where_to_find: Desert streams and pools in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank in shallow, clear water for flashing, tiny fish.

fun_fact: Lorquin's admiral often perches on a branch and chases off other butterflies that fly past.
where_to_find: Streamsides, woodland edges, willows and gardens in the West.
spotting_tip: Watch sunny trail edges near willows for dark wings with white and orange tips.

size: Colonies up to 2 ft wide (60 cm)
weight: Up to 10 lb (4.5 kg) for large colonies
fun_fact: A magnificent bryozoan looks like a jelly blob but is a colony of thousands of tiny animals.
where_to_find: Lakes, ponds and slow streams, attached to sticks and rocks.
spotting_tip: Look from the shore or a dock for a clear, jelly-like blob on submerged sticks.

fun_fact: This freshwater mussel is named for the bumpy ridges on its shell that look like maple leaf veins.
where_to_find: Muddy and sandy bottoms of rivers and large streams.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells on riverbanks and leave them where you find them.

fun_fact: This seabird nests high on mossy branches of old trees, far from the water where it feeds.
where_to_find: Coastal waters near old-growth forests along the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Scan calm bays from the shore at dawn with binoculars for small, dark seabirds.

fun_fact: This tiny hover fly looks like a wasp but cannot sting; the pattern on its back looks like writing.
where_to_find: Flower gardens, meadows and field edges.
spotting_tip: Watch small flowers for tiny, hovering, striped flies.

fun_fact: Marine blue caterpillars are often guarded by ants, which get a sweet liquid treat in return.
where_to_find: Gardens, dry washes, fields and desert flowers.
spotting_tip: Watch low flowers and bushes in sunny weather for tiny, lilac-blue butterflies.

fun_fact: Mayan cichlids guard their eggs and baby fish like caring parents.
where_to_find: Warm canals, ponds and marshes in southern waters.
spotting_tip: Look from a bridge or bank in clear shallow water for striped, orange-edged fish.

fun_fact: Geckos can climb walls and ceilings thanks to tiny hairs on their toes.
where_to_find: Walls and porches of buildings near lights, plus rocks and fences in warm areas.

fun_fact: Melissa blue caterpillars make a sweet liquid that ants love, and the ants protect them.
where_to_find: Prairies, meadows and open fields with legume flowers.
spotting_tip: Watch low wildflowers on warm days for tiny blue butterflies.

fun_fact: Mexican jays live in big family groups where aunts and older siblings help feed the babies.
where_to_find: Oak and pine woodlands in mountain canyons.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud calls in oak woods and look for blue-gray birds in groups.

fun_fact: Armadillos nearly always have four identical babies from a single egg.
where_to_find: Woodlands, brush, grasslands and garden edges across the South.
spotting_tip: Look at dusk along field edges for a snuffling animal digging for bugs; keep your distance.
safety_note: Never touch wild armadillos. Use zoom and keep hands clean.

fun_fact: Spadefoots spend most of the year buried underground and come up for big rains to breed.
where_to_find: Grasslands, deserts and sandy plains.
spotting_tip: Listen for chorusing after summer storms and view from the edge of temporary pools.

fun_fact: Milbert's tortoiseshell butterflies spend winter hiding as adults and wake up early in spring.
where_to_find: Meadows, streamsides and mountain trails.
spotting_tip: Look for orange-banded wings near nettle patches on sunny days.

fun_fact: The fuzzy caterpillars eat milkweed, the same plant monarch caterpillars use.
where_to_find: Meadows, roadsides and gardens with milkweed.
spotting_tip: Check milkweed leaves for fuzzy caterpillars from a distance and do not touch the hairs.

fun_fact: Mississippi kites catch dragonflies and other insects in midair and even eat them while flying.
where_to_find: Tall trees near rivers, woodland edges and neighborhoods in the plains.
spotting_tip: Look up on warm days for slender gray birds soaring on pointed wings.

fun_fact: When bothered, this salamander oozes a sticky, glue-like slime.
where_to_find: Damp hardwood forests and stream ravines.
spotting_tip: After rain, scan damp trails and forest floors from the path; never flip logs.

fun_fact: Moonglow anemones can fold in their tentacles and shrink when the tide goes out.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools in cold Pacific waters.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide and keep your hands to yourself.

fun_fact: The Moorish idol has a long, flowing fin that looks like a streamer.
where_to_find: Coral reefs and rocky reefs with warm, clear water.
spotting_tip: Snorkel safely with an adult and look for black, yellow and white striped fish.

where_to_find: Forests, wetlands, ponds and willow thickets in the North.

fun_fact: This butterfly's silvery-spotted underwings help it blend into mountain meadows.

fun_fact: This small lizard's eyes have see-through scales, like built-in goggles.
where_to_find: Rocky coasts, lava rock and shoreline plants.
spotting_tip: Scan warm rocks near the shore for a small, speckled lizard.

fun_fact: Mottled stars feed on mussels by slowly prying them open with their arms.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, tide pools and shallow bays.

fun_fact: Male mountain bluebirds are a bright sky blue, and they often hover over fields to find bugs.
where_to_find: Open meadows, sagebrush and mountain fields.
spotting_tip: Look at fence posts and open grassland for sky-blue birds.

fun_fact: Mountain chickadees hide seeds in fall and remember where they put them.

spotting_tip: Listen for a clear, whistled song and look in conifer branches.

fun_fact: Cottontails sit still to hide, then bolt with a zigzag run when a predator gets close.
where_to_find: Sagebrush, brush patches and rocky foothills.
spotting_tip: Scan brush edges at sunrise and sunset from a path.

size: 4–6 ft long (1.2–1.8 m), about 3.5 ft tall at shoulder (1.1 m)

where_to_find: Steep, rocky mountain slopes and alpine meadows.

safety_note: If you ever see a mountain lion, stay calm, stay with an adult and back away slowly.

fun_fact: Mountain whitefish are cold-water fish that often live in groups.
where_to_find: Cold, clear rivers and streams.
spotting_tip: Look from a bridge or bank in clear, cool water.

fun_fact: The whistling sound a mourning dove makes when it takes off comes from air rushing through its wing feathers.
where_to_find: Open woods, fields, farms, backyards and power lines.
spotting_tip: Look on wires and fences for plump, soft gray-brown birds with a long pointed tail.

fun_fact: Female mourning geckos can lay fertile eggs without a mate, so one gecko can start a whole group.
where_to_find: Gardens, buildings and trees in warm areas.
spotting_tip: View near outdoor lights from a distance, with an adult nearby.

fun_fact: Male fiddler crabs wave one giant claw to attract mates and scare rivals.
where_to_find: Salt marshes and muddy shores.
spotting_tip: Look at low tide from the marsh edge for crabs waving their big claw.

size: 6–8 ft long (1.8–2.4 m), about 4–5 ft tall at shoulder (1.2–1.5 m)

where_to_find: Arctic tundra and cold, windswept plains.

where_to_find: Ponds, marshes, ditches and slow streams.

fun_fact: Mute swans aren't silent; they hiss and snort, and their wings make a throbbing sound in flight.
where_to_find: Lakes, ponds, slow rivers and bays.
spotting_tip: Look on calm water for large white birds with orange beaks.
safety_note: Mute swans can be aggressive near nests. Use zoom and stay back.

fun_fact: After diving for fish, cormorants hold their wings out to dry because their feathers soak up water.
where_to_find: Lakes, ponds, bays and coastal waters.
spotting_tip: Scan posts and pilings for dark birds with wings spread out to dry.

fun_fact: A porcupine has about 30,000 quills, but it cannot shoot them.
where_to_find: Forests and wooded areas, especially in the North.
spotting_tip: Look high in trees for a round, dark shape and enjoy it from far away.
safety_note: A porcupine's quills can hurt a lot. Keep pets away and use zoom.

fun_fact: Racers are very fast, and young racers have blotches that fade to a solid color as they grow.
where_to_find: Fields, forest edges, brush and open woods.

safety_note: Racers can bite if cornered. Use zoom and step back.

fun_fact: The wheel bug has a cog-wheel crest on its back and uses a long beak to eat other insects.

safety_note: Wheel bugs can give a painful bite. Use zoom and never touch.

fun_fact: Barnacles are crustaceans related to crabs, and they glue themselves to rocks for life.
where_to_find: Rocky shores in the tide zone.
spotting_tip: Look on rocks at low tide for white cone-shaped shells; stay off the slippery spots.

fun_fact: Northern alligator lizards can drop their tails if caught and grow a new one.
where_to_find: Forests, meadows and rocky slopes.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny logs and rocks quietly from a distance.

fun_fact: Mussels attach to rocks with strong threads and filter food from the water.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools.
spotting_tip: Look on rocks at low tide for dark blue shells packed together.

fun_fact: Cottonmouths open their mouths wide to show a white inside as a warning to back off.
where_to_find: Swamps, slow rivers, ponds and marshy edges.
spotting_tip: Scan water edges with zoom from the path and never wade through swampy water.
safety_note: Cottonmouths are venomous. Never approach, and walk away calmly if you see one.

fun_fact: Its call sounds like two marbles clicking together, getting faster and faster.
where_to_find: Edges of ponds, streams and marshes.
spotting_tip: Listen for clicking calls near pond edges on warm days.

fun_fact: The curly-tailed lizard curls its tail over its back like a question mark.
where_to_find: Rocky areas, sandy lots and coastal scrub.
spotting_tip: Look on rocks and walls in sunny areas for a lizard with a curled tail.

fun_fact: This salamander breathes through its skin and needs to stay damp.
where_to_find: Wet rocks and mossy banks beside forest streams.
spotting_tip: After rain, look along stream edges from a trail; never flip rocks.

size: 16–20 in long (41–51 cm), wingspan about 42 in (107 cm)
fun_fact: Northern harriers hunt with their ears as much as their eyes, thanks to an owl-like face.
where_to_find: Marshes, grasslands and open fields.
spotting_tip: Look for a low-flying hawk with a white rump patch gliding over a field.

fun_fact: Small and loud, the house wren sings a bubbly song and nests in birdhouses.
where_to_find: Backyards, woodland edges and brushy areas.
spotting_tip: Listen for a bubbling song in shrubs and spot a small brown bird with its tail raised.

size: Shell up to 4 in wide (10 cm)
fun_fact: Kelp crabs decorate themselves with seaweed to blend in.
where_to_find: Kelp beds, rocky shores and tide pools.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide for a smooth, olive-colored crab.

fun_fact: Leopard frogs jump away in a zigzag path to confuse predators.
where_to_find: Wet meadows, ponds, marshes and slow streams.
spotting_tip: Walk quietly beside pond edges and look for green frogs with dark spots.

fun_fact: Its shell pattern looks like a map of squiggly lines.
where_to_find: Large rivers and lakes.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and rocks in the water for basking turtles from far away.

fun_fact: Paper wasps chew wood into pulp to make papery nests.
where_to_find: Gardens, porches, eaves and wooded edges.
spotting_tip: Look for small paper nests from a distance and never touch them.
safety_note: Wasps can sting if their nest is bothered. Walk away calmly.

fun_fact: Northern pike are fast ambush predators with a mouthful of sharp teeth.
where_to_find: Cool lakes, weedy bays and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Look from a dock or shore in weedy shallows for a long, green fish.

fun_fact: Pintails have long, elegant tails and can travel thousands of miles each year.
where_to_find: Marshes, ponds and flooded fields.
spotting_tip: Look for ducks with long pointed tails in shallow open water.

fun_fact: Despite the name, this turtle's belly color ranges from yellow to red-pink.
where_to_find: Ponds, slow rivers and tidal marshes.
spotting_tip: Scan logs in the water for large basking turtles.

fun_fact: Red-legged frogs have a red wash under their legs and often hide in damp woods.
where_to_find: Damp forests and ponds.
spotting_tip: After rain, scan pond edges from the trail without touching.

fun_fact: Rubber boas have a short blunt tail that looks like a head, which confuses predators.
where_to_find: Forests, meadows and rocky hillsides.
spotting_tip: Snakes are rarely seen; keep to the trail and enjoy looking for signs from afar.

fun_fact: This shrew has venom in its saliva that helps it hunt larger prey.
where_to_find: Forests, fields and brush.
spotting_tip: Look for small tunnels in leaf litter and keep to the trail.
safety_note: Shrews can bite. Use zoom and never touch.

fun_fact: The shoveler's huge spoon-shaped bill filters tiny food from water.
where_to_find: Shallow marshes and ponds.
spotting_tip: Look for ducks with large bills sweeping them side to side in shallow water.

fun_fact: When picked up by a predator, it oozes sticky slime that is hard to wash off.
where_to_find: Damp forests and rocky slopes.
spotting_tip: After rain, look from the trail on forest floors; never flip rocks.

fun_fact: Two-lined salamanders lay eggs under rocks in clear streams.
where_to_find: Rocky brooks and wet woods.
spotting_tip: Look near stream edges from the trail; never flip rocks.

fun_fact: Yellow warblers sometimes build a new nest floor on top of an unwanted cowbird egg.
where_to_find: Willows, wetlands and streamsides.
spotting_tip: Listen for a sweet song and scan willows for a bright yellow bird.

fun_fact: Some zigzag salamanders have a wiggly stripe down their backs, while others have none.
where_to_find: Damp woods and rocky slopes.
spotting_tip: After rain, look from the trail; never flip rocks.

fun_fact: Garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
where_to_find: Meadows, gardens, forests and wet edges.
spotting_tip: Watch sunny paths from a distance for slender striped snakes.

fun_fact: Some northwestern salamanders keep their gills as adults.
where_to_find: Ponds, damp woods and lakes.
spotting_tip: After rain, look at pond edges from the trail without touching.

fun_fact: Pill woodlice are crustaceans and many can roll into a ball for protection.
where_to_find: Damp leaf litter, gardens and wooded yards.
spotting_tip: Look for small gray pill bugs in damp spots from a distance.

fun_fact: The lady crab has flat paddle legs and can swim and burrow quickly.
where_to_find: Sandy ocean shores and shallow bays.
spotting_tip: Look in shallow sandy water from the shore for spotted crabs.

fun_fact: Its orange crown patch is rarely seen; this warbler is a dull olive-yellow.
where_to_find: Brushy woods, thickets and edges.
spotting_tip: Look in shrubs and willows for small greenish birds.

fun_fact: Orange sea cucumbers catch food from the water with feathery tentacles.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and cold shallows.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools at low tide for orange tentacles from the edge.

fun_fact: Male orangespotted sunfish are covered with bright orange spots during breeding.
where_to_find: Warm, muddy streams and ponds.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank in shallow pools for small, bright fish.

fun_fact: Male orangethroat darters turn bright orange and blue in spring.
where_to_find: Clear, gravelly creeks.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank in riffles for small, colorful fish.

fun_fact: Orcas are the largest dolphins and hunt in family groups called pods.
where_to_find: Cold coastal waters, bays and open ocean.
spotting_tip: Watch from shore, ferries or tour boats for tall black fins.
safety_note: Orcas are wild animals. Watch from far away or on an official whale tour.

fun_fact: The oriental beetle's grubs live underground and eat roots.
where_to_find: Lawns, gardens and flowers.
spotting_tip: Look on garden flowers at dusk without touching.

fun_fact: Box turtles can close their shells tight like a box.
where_to_find: Prairies, grasslands and sandy fields.
spotting_tip: Look carefully on grassy trails and let turtles go on their way.

fun_fact: Males flash blue patches on their bellies to show off.
where_to_find: Rocky slopes, trees and desert washes.
spotting_tip: Scan warm rocks and trunks from a distance.

fun_fact: Like other lungless salamanders, it breathes through its skin.
where_to_find: Damp hardwood forests, caves and rocky slopes.
spotting_tip: After rain, look on the trail edge; never flip rocks.

fun_fact: Banana slugs are among the largest slugs in the world and help forests by eating leaf litter.
where_to_find: Damp redwood and other forests.
spotting_tip: Look on damp forest floors after rain from the trail.

fun_fact: Its ribbit is the classic frog sound heard in many movies.
where_to_find: Ponds, meadows, gardens and wet forests.
spotting_tip: Listen for choruses at dusk near ponds.

fun_fact: This is one of the largest land salamanders in North America and can even make a barking sound.
where_to_find: Cold streams in damp forests.
spotting_tip: After rain, look near stream edges from the trail; never flip rocks.

fun_fact: Pacific golden plovers fly thousands of miles over the ocean to reach Hawaii each year.
where_to_find: Grassy fields, mudflats and shorelines.
spotting_tip: Scan lawns and mudflats for speckled gold birds.

weight: Up to 50 lb (23 kg) for large ones
fun_fact: Its tentacles trail like a lion's mane and can be very long.
where_to_find: Cold ocean waters and bays.
spotting_tip: Look from a dock or boat; do not touch washed-up jellies.
safety_note: Jelly tentacles can sting even when washed up. Never touch.

fun_fact: Loons dive deep underwater to catch fish.

spotting_tip: Scan calm water with binoculars for sleek diving birds.

fun_fact: Orange spines near its tail are used for defense.
where_to_find: Coral reefs and rocky reefs.
spotting_tip: Snorkel with an adult and look for gray fish with an orange tail spine.

fun_fact: Pacific sideband snails use a rasping tongue to scrape their food.

fun_fact: Sea cucumbers help clean the seafloor by eating tiny bits of debris.

spotting_tip: Look while snorkeling with an adult; never pick them up.

fun_fact: Painted anemones are colorful and use stinging tentacles to catch small animals.
