fun_fact: Painted turtles can survive winter under frozen ponds.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Scan logs in the water for basking turtles from the shore.

fun_fact: This grasshopper snaps its wings in flight and blends into the ground.
where_to_find: Dry open ground, deserts and roadsides.
spotting_tip: Watch the ground ahead for a gray grasshopper that pops up and flies.

fun_fact: The palm warbler constantly wags its tail up and down.
where_to_find: Open fields, parks and scrubby edges in winter.
spotting_tip: Look low on the ground and shrubs for a tail-wagging bird.

fun_fact: This chipmunk lives only in one small mountain range.
where_to_find: Rocky pine and fir forest in the high mountains.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and rocky ground in high-elevation forests.

fun_fact: Pantropical spotted dolphins are born without spots and gain more as they age.
where_to_find: Warm ocean waters, bays and open sea.
spotting_tip: Watch from boat tours or shore for fast, leaping dolphins.

fun_fact: The pearl crescent butterfly is named for the pale crescent on the edge of its hindwing.
where_to_find: Fields, meadows and gardens.
spotting_tip: Look on low flowers for small orange butterflies.

fun_fact: Pelagic cormorants nest on narrow cliff ledges and dive for fish.
where_to_find: Rocky coasts and cliffs.
spotting_tip: Scan sea cliffs and rocks for slim dark birds.

fun_fact: Males have bright orange-red heads for showing off.
where_to_find: Rocks, walls and open sunny areas.
spotting_tip: Look on sunny walls and rocks for bright-headed lizards.

fun_fact: Phainopeplas eat desert mistletoe berries and spread the seeds.

spotting_tip: Look for glossy black birds on treetops.

fun_fact: The pickerel frog's skin gives off a mild toxin that protects it from predators.
where_to_find: Wet meadows, ponds and cool streams.
spotting_tip: Look near pond edges from the trail; do not touch the frogs.

fun_fact: Pied-billed grebes can sink slowly below the surface without diving.
where_to_find: Ponds, marshes and lakes.
spotting_tip: Look for small brown swimmers on calm water.

fun_fact: Its bright red feet and white wing patches make it easy to spot.
where_to_find: Rocky coastlines and cliffs.
spotting_tip: Scan rocky shores for black birds with white wing patches.

fun_fact: Pine siskins travel in flocks and can show up at feeders in winter.
where_to_find: Conifer forests and backyard feeders.
spotting_tip: Check feeders for small streaky finches with yellow wing flashes.

fun_fact: Pine warblers eat seeds in winter, which few warblers do.
where_to_find: Pine forests across the Southeast.
spotting_tip: Listen for trilling songs in pines and look up for yellowish birds.

fun_fact: Pink salmon live only two years and return to the stream where they were born.
where_to_find: Cold ocean waters and gravelly streams.
spotting_tip: Look from a bridge or bank in streams for fish swimming upstream.

fun_fact: This non-venomous snake has a plain, bright belly and eats frogs and fish.
where_to_find: Streams, ponds and wet woods.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny banks and logs from a distance.
safety_note: Watersnakes can bite if cornered. Use zoom and never touch.

fun_fact: Pocketbook mussels use a lure that looks like a little fish to attract host fish.
where_to_find: Rivers and lakes with sandy bottoms.
spotting_tip: Look for empty shells on riverbanks; leave them in place.

fun_fact: Plains garter snakes eat earthworms and live near water.
where_to_find: Prairies, meadows and wet areas.
spotting_tip: Watch grassy edges near water from a distance.

fun_fact: Hognose snakes play dead and flatten their necks like cobras to scare predators.
where_to_find: Prairies, sandy soils and dry grasslands.
spotting_tip: Scan sandy grassland paths from a distance.

fun_fact: Plains leopard frogs have a ridge on each side that makes them easy to recognize.
where_to_find: Prairie ponds, wet fields and streams.
spotting_tip: Walk quietly along pond edges and scan for spotted frogs.

fun_fact: Plains longear sunfish have bright colors and long, flap-like gill covers.
where_to_find: Clear streams and small rivers.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank in clear, shallow water.

fun_fact: Plains spadefoots dig backward into the ground with spade-like feet.
where_to_find: Grasslands, sandy soils and temporary pools.
spotting_tip: Listen for calls after heavy rain and view from the pool edge.

fun_fact: Fence lizards do push-ups to show off their territory.
where_to_find: Rocky slopes, woodland edges and fences.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny rocks and fences from a distance.

fun_fact: Whiptail lizards run fast and stop for only a second.
where_to_find: Dry hillsides, rocky slopes and grasslands.
spotting_tip: Look for fast striped lizards on warm rocks.

fun_fact: Polynesian rats were brought to Hawaii by early voyagers long ago.
where_to_find: Forests, fields and near buildings.
spotting_tip: This animal is shy; look for it from a distance during daylight.
safety_note: Wild rats can bite and carry germs. Never touch them.

size: Float 3–6 in long (8–15 cm), tentacles up to 30 ft (9 m) or more
fun_fact: A Portuguese man o' war is not a single animal but a colony of tiny animals working together.
where_to_find: Warm ocean surface and beaches after storms.
spotting_tip: If you see a blue float on the beach, look but do not touch and tell an adult.
safety_note: The tentacles can sting even when washed up. Never touch one and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Male prairie lizards flash bright blue patches on their bellies to show off to rivals.
where_to_find: Dry open woods, rocky clearings and grasslands across the central US.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny logs, fence posts and rocks from a distance; they dart away fast.

fun_fact: Rattlesnakes sense warm animals with special heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils.
where_to_find: Dry grasslands, prairie dog towns and rocky hillsides across the Great Plains and Rockies.
active_time: Daytime in spring and fall, evening in summer
spotting_tip: Watch the trail ahead and listen for the rattle; never approach.
safety_note: Never touch or try to move a rattlesnake. Use zoom and step back the way you came.

fun_fact: Young prairie skinks have bright blue tails, and like many lizards they can drop their tails to escape.
where_to_find: Sandy prairies, open woods and rocky hillsides in the northern Midwest.
spotting_tip: Look for a quick shiny flash near sunny rocks and logs, and watch from a distance.

size: 3.5–5 ft long (1.1–1.5 m), about 3 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Pronghorn can run over 50 mph, making them the fastest land animal in North America.
where_to_find: Open grasslands, sagebrush plains and high desert across the West.
spotting_tip: Scan wide open plains with binoculars; look for white rumps flashing as they run.
safety_note: Wild animals can be unpredictable. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Male pumpkinseeds fan out a shallow nest in the sandy bottom and guard their eggs.
where_to_find: Calm, weedy ponds, lakes and slow streams across the North.
spotting_tip: Look from docks and shorelines into clear shallows, where they hover near plants.

fun_fact: Purple gallinules have very long toes that let them walk on top of floating lily pads.
where_to_find: Freshwater marshes and ponds with floating plants in Florida.
spotting_tip: Scan lily pads and reeds at the water's edge for a bright blue and purple bird.

fun_fact: Despite the name, purple shore crabs can be purple, green or reddish, often with purple spots on the claws.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools along the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Watch rocky tide pools at low tide from the shore, and never turn rocks over on yourself.

fun_fact: Horned lizards can give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
where_to_find: Dry sagebrush flats and open rocky ground in eastern Washington.
spotting_tip: Scan bare patches of sandy ground; their flat bodies blend in so look for slow movement.

fun_fact: Queen butterflies are close cousins of monarchs and taste bad to birds, just like them.
where_to_find: Desert washes, fields and gardens with milkweed in the Southwest and Texas.
spotting_tip: Look for orange-brown butterflies on milkweed and flowers, and watch from a distance.

fun_fact: In spring, male rainbow darters glow with blue, green and orange stripes.
where_to_find: Clear, rocky, fast-flowing creeks and streams in the eastern and central US.
spotting_tip: Look into clear, shallow riffles from the bank for small fish resting on the stream bottom.

fun_fact: Rainbow trout that migrate to the sea are called steelhead and grow much bigger than stream trout.
where_to_find: Cold, clear rivers, streams and lakes across the West.
spotting_tip: Look into clear pools from a bridge or bank, where trout face upstream.

fun_fact: Woodlice are not insects; they are crustaceans, related to crabs and shrimp.
where_to_find: Damp leaf litter, gardens and wood piles across the Midwest and North.
spotting_tip: Look gently around damp mulch and leaves, and leave them where you found them.

fun_fact: Red admirals often migrate long distances, flying south for the winter.
where_to_find: Gardens, woodland edges, parks and wet fields across the US.
spotting_tip: Check flowers and tree sap on sunny days and watch quietly from a distance.

fun_fact: Red beard sponges filter the water, and their bright orange to red fingers look like a beard.
where_to_find: Shallow bays, docks and pilings along the Atlantic coast.
spotting_tip: Look for orange fingers on docks and pilings at low tide, and do not touch.

fun_fact: Red-bellied snakes are tiny and eat slugs, which gardeners are glad to be rid of.
where_to_find: Moist woods, forest edges and meadows across the North and East.
spotting_tip: Watch the edges of damp trails and leaf litter; never pick them up.

fun_fact: Bumble bees buzz their flight muscles to shake pollen loose from flowers, which is called buzz pollination.
where_to_find: Meadows, prairies and flower-filled gardens across the northern US.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers from a few steps back and look for the orange band on the body.
safety_note: Bees sting if bothered. Use zoom and stay calm.

fun_fact: Red-billed leiothrix are originally from Asia, and they sing a lovely, flute-like song.
where_to_find: Forests and thickets in the mountains of Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Listen for cheerful songs in dense bushes and scan for a bright red-orange bill.

fun_fact: Red-breasted mergansers have shaggy crests and thin bills with tiny toothlike edges for catching fish.
where_to_find: Coastal bays, lakes and large rivers across the North and coasts.
spotting_tip: Scan open water from shore with binoculars and look for a shaggy-headed duck diving for fish.

fun_fact: Red-breasted nuthatches climb down tree trunks headfirst, and they smear sticky tree sap around their nest holes.
where_to_find: Evergreen forests across the North and West, and backyards with feeders.
spotting_tip: Listen for tiny nasal 'yank yank' calls and look on trunks of pines and spruces.

fun_fact: Despite the name, the red-crested cardinal is not a true cardinal; it is a type of tanager from South America.
where_to_find: Lawns, parks and gardens in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan lawns and low bushes in parks for a gray bird with a bright red head and crest.

fun_fact: Red-footed boobies are expert fishers that dive into the ocean to catch flying fish and squid.
where_to_find: Seacoasts, cliffs and offshore islands in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan coastal cliffs and the sky over the ocean with binoculars from a safe viewpoint.

fun_fact: Red-headed woodpeckers hide acorns and insects in tree cracks to eat later in winter.
where_to_find: Open woods, orchards and farmland with dead trees across the central and eastern US.
spotting_tip: Look for a bold black, white and red bird on dead trees or fence posts.

fun_fact: Red-necked grebes perform dancing displays on the water, and their chicks often ride on a parent's back.
where_to_find: Marshy lakes and ponds in Alaska.
spotting_tip: Scan quiet lakes with binoculars and look for a duck-sized bird with a dagger-shaped bill.

fun_fact: Red-necked phalaropes spin in circles on the water to stir up tiny food, and the females are more colorful than the males.
where_to_find: Tundra ponds in summer and open ocean waters in Alaska.
spotting_tip: Look for small birds spinning in circles on shallow ponds.

fun_fact: Red rock crabs have strong claws with black tips that can crack open shells.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, tide pools and kelp beds along the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Watch tide pools at low tide from a safe spot and keep fingers away from claws.

fun_fact: Male red shiners flush with bright red and blue colors during the breeding season.
where_to_find: Muddy creeks and prairie streams across the Great Plains.
spotting_tip: Look into shallow stream pools from the bank for small flashing silver fish.

fun_fact: Red-spotted toads make a musical, bird-like trill after rain.
where_to_find: Rocky canyons, desert streams and springs in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Listen for trills near desert streams after rain, and watch with an adult.

fun_fact: Red swamp crayfish can survive dry spells by burrowing deep into mud.
where_to_find: Swamps, ditches, ponds and rice fields in the South and West.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank into shallow muddy water for a red crayfish.

size: 28–38 in long (71–97 cm), including tail streamers
fun_fact: Red-tailed tropicbirds have two long red tail streamers and can dive into the ocean from high up.
where_to_find: Sea cliffs and open ocean waters of Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan the sky above sea cliffs with binoculars for a white bird with red streamers.

fun_fact: Red-vented bulbuls have a bright red patch under the tail and a cheerful, bubbly song.
where_to_find: Gardens, parks and forest edges in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan treetops and shrubs in parks for a dark bird with a crest and a red patch.

fun_fact: Redbreast sunfish have long black 'ear' flaps and bright orange bellies.
where_to_find: Rivers, streams and clear lakes along the Atlantic coast and Southeast.
spotting_tip: Look from a bank or bridge in clear water near fallen logs and rocks.

fun_fact: Male stag beetles have large jaws like antlers that they use to wrestle each other, but they are harmless to people.
where_to_find: Woodlands with old logs and stumps in the Northeast.
spotting_tip: Look near rotting logs and porch lights on summer evenings, and leave them alone.

fun_fact: Male redline darters have bright orange lines along their sides during breeding season.
where_to_find: Clear, rocky, fast-moving streams in Tennessee.
spotting_tip: Look into clear, shallow riffles from the bank for small colorful fish.

fun_fact: Redpolls can survive cold nights by tunneling into snow for warmth.
where_to_find: Tundra, birch woods and brushy fields in Alaska.
spotting_tip: Look for flocks of small streaky birds with red caps at feeders and in birch trees.

fun_fact: Redside shiners turn bright red along their sides in the breeding season.
where_to_find: Cool lakes and slow rivers in the northern Rockies.
spotting_tip: Look from docks and shorelines into clear shallow water for schools of small fish.

fun_fact: The relict leopard frog was thought to be extinct for decades before it was rediscovered.
where_to_find: Desert springs and marshes in southern Nevada.
spotting_tip: Never disturb its wet habitat; look from a distance with an adult.

fun_fact: Richardson's ground squirrels stand up on their back legs and whistle to warn others about danger.
where_to_find: Open grasslands and prairies in North Dakota.
spotting_tip: Scan open prairie for upright squirrels near burrow mounds.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite. Never feed them. Use zoom.

fun_fact: Ring-billed gulls have a black ring around the bill, and they are often seen far from the ocean.
where_to_find: Lakes, parks, parking lots and coasts across the US.
spotting_tip: Look at shorelines, beaches and parking lots, and watch from a distance.

fun_fact: The ring on a ring-necked duck is hard to see; the white ring on its bill is much easier to spot.
where_to_find: Ponds, lakes and marshes in the West.
spotting_tip: Scan quiet freshwater ponds for a dark duck with a white-ringed bill.

fun_fact: Male ring-necked pheasants have bright feathers and a loud crow, and the species was brought to North America from Asia.
where_to_find: Farm fields, grasslands and brushy edges in the northern Plains.
spotting_tip: Scan field edges and ditches at sunrise for a colorful long-tailed bird.

fun_fact: Ring-necked snakes curl their tails to show a bright red-orange underside when scared.
where_to_find: Moist woods, rocky hillsides and gardens across much of the US.
spotting_tip: Watch edges of woods and rocky trails from a distance without touching.
safety_note: Do not touch snakes you can't identify. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Rio Grande leopard frogs make a chuckling call that sounds like a short laugh.
where_to_find: Ponds, ditches and slow streams in southern Texas.
spotting_tip: Listen for chuckling calls near ponds after dark and look from the bank.

fun_fact: River cooters love to bask on logs in the sun, stacked on top of each other.
where_to_find: Rivers, lakes and slow streams in the South.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny logs in the water from a bank or bridge with binoculars.

fun_fact: Rivoli's hummingbirds are one of the largest hummingbirds in the US, and the males flash bright green and purple.
where_to_find: Mountain canyons and gardens with feeders in southern Arizona.
spotting_tip: Watch hummingbird feeders and flowers from a quiet spot and look for a big dark hummingbird.

fun_fact: Rock bass have red-orange eyes that stand out against their dark bodies.
where_to_find: Clear streams, rocky lakes and rivers in the East and Midwest.
spotting_tip: Look near rocks and logs from a bank or dock in clear water.

fun_fact: Rock squirrels are skilled climbers that scamper up cliffs and boulders and can even climb trees.
where_to_find: Rocky hillsides, canyons and desert foothills in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Scan boulders and cliff edges for squirrels sitting upright in the sun.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite. Never feed them. Use zoom.

fun_fact: Cutthroat trout get their name from the red-orange slash on each side of the lower jaw.
where_to_find: Cold, clear mountain streams and lakes in the Rocky Mountains.
spotting_tip: Look into clear pools from the bank with polarized sunglasses and stay quiet.

fun_fact: Rocky Mountain parnassians live high in the mountains, and the caterpillars eat stonecrop plants.
where_to_find: High mountain meadows and rocky slopes in the Rockies.
spotting_tip: Look for white and red-spotted butterflies on mountain wildflowers on sunny days.

fun_fact: Tailed frogs live in fast icy mountain streams, and their 'tail' is actually used by males to mate.
where_to_find: Cold, clear, fast mountain streams in the northern Rockies.
spotting_tip: Never disturb streams; look from the bank with an adult.

fun_fact: Male rose-breasted grosbeaks have a bright rose patch on the chest and sing a song like a robin.
where_to_find: Woodland edges, parks and backyards with feeders in the Upper Midwest.
spotting_tip: Scan treetops in spring and look for a black and white bird with a pink chest patch.

fun_fact: Rose-ringed parakeets can mimic human words, and the males have a thin pink and black ring around their necks.
where_to_find: Parks and neighborhoods with tall trees in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud shrieks and scan treetops in parks for a bright green parrot.

fun_fact: Roseate spoonbills get their pink color from the tiny crustaceans they eat.
where_to_find: Coastal mangroves, marshes and shallow ponds in Florida.
spotting_tip: Scan shallow wetlands from a boardwalk or overlook for a pink bird sweeping its bill side to side.

fun_fact: Rosy maple moths are fuzzy pink and yellow, which makes them look like a scoop of sherbet.
where_to_find: Forests and neighborhoods with maple trees in the Northeast.
spotting_tip: Look near porch lights on summer evenings and watch with an adult.

fun_fact: Rough earthsnakes give birth to live babies and spend most of their time hiding under leaves.
where_to_find: Moist woods, gardens and leaf litter in Texas.
spotting_tip: Watch edges of damp trails from a distance and don't flip rocks onto yourself.

fun_fact: Rough harvester ants collect seeds and clear bare circles around their nest entrance.
where_to_find: Dry deserts and grasslands in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Look for a bare circle of ground with ants streaming in and out and keep a few steps back.
safety_note: These ants have a painful sting. Do not step on their nests; use zoom.

fun_fact: Rough-skinned newts have a toxic skin that makes them unpleasant for predators to eat.
where_to_find: Ponds, forests and damp trails along the Pacific coast.
spotting_tip: Watch damp trails and ponds from a distance; never touch one.
safety_note: Newt skin is toxic. Do not touch, and wash hands if you do. Use zoom.

fun_fact: Round gobies have fused fins that act like a suction cup for sticking to rocks.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and lake bottoms of the Great Lakes.
spotting_tip: Look into clear water near rocks and docks from the shore.

fun_fact: Round-tailed ground squirrels stay cool in the desert by lying flat on cool soil and burrowing underground.
where_to_find: Sandy desert flats and scrub in southern Arizona.
spotting_tip: Scan sandy areas near burrows in the morning for squirrels standing upright.
safety_note: Wild rodents can bite. Never feed them. Use zoom.

fun_fact: Horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes to scare predators.
where_to_find: Dry grasslands, deserts and rocky hillsides in New Mexico.
spotting_tip: Scan bare ground slowly; their camouflage is excellent so look for small movement.

fun_fact: Ruby-crowned kinglets are tiny yet sing a loud song, and males flash a red crown when excited.
where_to_find: Woodlands, thickets and backyards in winter in the Southeast.
spotting_tip: Look for a tiny constantly flicking bird in shrubs and tree branches.

fun_fact: Ruddy ducks hold their tails up straight and the males put on a bubbling display.
where_to_find: Marshes, ponds and lakes in the West and northern Plains.
spotting_tip: Scan open ponds with binoculars for a small, round duck with a stiff tail.

fun_fact: Ruddy turnstones flip over stones and seaweed to find food, which is how they got their name.
where_to_find: Rocky shores, beaches and jetties along the coast.
spotting_tip: Look along the tide line on beaches and jetties for orange-legged shorebirds.

fun_fact: Male ruffed grouse beat their wings to make a drumming sound that you can feel in your chest.
where_to_find: Young woods and forest edges in the Rockies.
spotting_tip: Listen for deep drumming in spring and scan quiet forest trails from a distance.

fun_fact: Millipedes do not actually have 1,000 legs, but they do have many pairs on each body segment.
where_to_find: Damp gardens, leaf litter and mulch in Florida.
spotting_tip: Look at damp ground in gardens from a distance and don't pick them up.
safety_note: Millipedes can release an irritating fluid. Look but don't touch.

fun_fact: Saddle wrasses change color as they grow, and the males have bright orange and blue colors.
where_to_find: Coral reefs and rocky shallow waters in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Look through a mask or glass-bottom boat at reefs with an adult.

fun_fact: Saffron finches are bright yellow, and the males have an orange cap.
where_to_find: Parks, lawns and fields in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan grassy areas and fence lines for a bright yellow songbird.

fun_fact: The male sailfin molly raises a large sail-like fin to impress females.
where_to_find: Brackish marshes, coastal ponds and canals in the South.
spotting_tip: Look into calm coastal water and ponds for small fish with tall back fins.

fun_fact: The caterpillar of the salt marsh moth is covered in fuzzy hairs and is called a woolly bear.
where_to_find: Fields, gardens and marsh edges in Texas.
spotting_tip: Look near porch lights at night with an adult and watch from a distance.

fun_fact: Sanderlings run back and forth at the edge of waves like wind-up toys to catch tiny food.
where_to_find: Sandy beaches and shorelines along the coast.
spotting_tip: Watch the edge of the waves for small pale birds that follow every wave in and out.

fun_fact: Sandhill cranes do loud, rattling duets and dance with leaps and bows.
where_to_find: Wet meadows, marshes, prairies and farm fields across the country.
spotting_tip: Scan large open fields and wet meadows from a distance, and listen for rolling bugle calls.
safety_note: Cranes can be defensive and have a sharp bill. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Savannah sparrows have yellow near the eyes and sing a thin, buzzy song.
where_to_find: Open tundra, meadows and grasslands in Alaska.
spotting_tip: Scan fence posts and grassy fields for a streaky little bird with a yellow eyebrow.

fun_fact: Say's phoebes catch insects in midair and wag their tails when they perch.
where_to_find: Open deserts, ranches and farmland in the Southwest.
spotting_tip: Look for a gray-brown bird with an orange belly perched on fences and buildings.

fun_fact: Scaly-breasted munias build ball-shaped nests of grass and often hang around in noisy flocks.
where_to_find: Grasslands, farmland and road edges in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan grassy fields for little flocks of brown birds with scaly patterns on the chest.

fun_fact: Scissor-tailed flycatchers have very long tails that open and close like scissors in flight.
where_to_find: Open ranchland, roadsides and prairies in the southern Plains.
spotting_tip: Scan fences and power lines in open country for a pale bird with a long forked tail.

fun_fact: Seaside dragonlets live where saltwater meets land and are among the few dragonflies tolerant of salty water.
where_to_find: Salt marshes, beaches and coastal ponds on the Atlantic coast.
spotting_tip: Look at sunny marsh edges and tidal flats for small dark dragonflies perched on the ground.

fun_fact: Seven-spotted lady beetles eat aphids, which makes them helpful in gardens.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows and fields in the West and North.
spotting_tip: Look on plant leaves and stems in gardens and meadows from a few steps back.

fun_fact: The shark eye snail gets its name from the swirl on its shell that looks like an eye.
where_to_find: Sandy and muddy beaches along the Atlantic coast.
spotting_tip: Look along the beach at low tide for round swirl-shaped shells.

fun_fact: Shingle urchins hold on tight in crashing waves with flat spines that look like roof shingles.
where_to_find: Wave-splashed rocky shores in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Look from a safe, dry spot on rocky shores and never go near big waves.

fun_fact: Short-billed gulls have a small, gentle-looking yellow bill and a white, dark-eyed face.
where_to_find: Lakes, rivers, coasts and tundra in Alaska.
spotting_tip: Scan shorelines and docks with binoculars for a medium-sized gull.

fun_fact: Signal crayfish get their name from the white-blue spot on their claws that looks like a signal.
where_to_find: Cold clear streams, rivers and lakes in the Northwest.
spotting_tip: Look from the bank into clear shallow water around rocks.

size: 3.5–4 ft long (1.1–1.2 m), about 2.5–3 ft tall
fun_fact: Sika deer have white spots on their coats and make odd whistling calls.
where_to_find: Marshes, woods and coastal wetlands in Maryland.
spotting_tip: Scan forest and marsh edges at sunrise and dusk with binoculars.
safety_note: Deer can be unpredictable, especially in fall. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Silver-spotted skippers have a bright silver patch on their wings and a speedy, darting flight.
where_to_find: Gardens, meadows and woodland edges across the East and Midwest.
spotting_tip: Look on flowers on sunny days for a brown butterfly with a silver patch.

fun_fact: Six-lined racerunners are among the fastest lizards in the eastern US.
where_to_find: Sandy fields, dunes and dry open areas in the Midwest.
spotting_tip: Scan sandy open areas on sunny days for a speedy lizard with six pale stripes.

fun_fact: Mongooses were brought to Hawaii in the 1880s to control rats, but they now threaten native birds.
where_to_find: Sugar cane fields, forests and brushy areas in Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Scan roadsides and fields from your car or trail for a quick, slender animal.
safety_note: Mongooses can bite. Use zoom and stay with an adult.

fun_fact: Small whites have white wings with a gray spot, and they are one of the most common butterflies in gardens.
where_to_find: Gardens, farm fields and meadows across the US.
spotting_tip: Look over garden plants and fields for a small white fluttering butterfly.

fun_fact: Small wood-nymphs have eyespots on their wings that help startle hungry birds.
where_to_find: Grassy meadows and sagebrush foothills in the Rockies.
spotting_tip: Look for brown butterflies fluttering low over grassy meadows.

fun_fact: Male smallmouth bass guard their nest and baby fish for weeks.
where_to_find: Clear, rocky rivers and lakes across the East and Midwest.
spotting_tip: Look from a bank or bridge into clear water near rocks.

fun_fact: Smooth greensnakes are bright green, and they eat insects and spiders.
where_to_find: Damp meadows, grasslands and woodland edges in the North.
spotting_tip: Watch grassy edges and meadow trails; they blend in so look carefully but don't touch.

fun_fact: Snow geese fly in huge flocks thousands strong along their migration route.
where_to_find: Coastal marshes, bays and farm fields along the East coast.
spotting_tip: Scan wide fields and marshes for big flocks of white geese with black wingtips.

fun_fact: Snowshoe hares turn white in winter and brown in summer, and their big hind feet work like snowshoes.
where_to_find: Northern forests and thick brushy woods.
spotting_tip: Look at forest edges at twilight, and notice tracks in snow from a distance.

fun_fact: Snowy egrets have bright yellow feet that they sometimes wiggle to stir up fish.
where_to_find: Marshes, shallow coastal waters and ponds across the South and East coast.
spotting_tip: Scan shallow water and tidal flats for a white heron with a black bill and yellow feet.

fun_fact: Sockeye salmon turn bright red when they return to rivers to spawn.
where_to_find: Cold rivers, lakes and the North Pacific.
spotting_tip: Watch the salmon run from a viewing platform or bridge in late summer.

fun_fact: Each male song sparrow sings many different songs, and each has a different set.
where_to_find: Backyards, thickets, marshes and field edges across the US.
spotting_tip: Listen for a cheerful song from a bush and look for a streaky brown bird with a central chest spot.

fun_fact: The Sonoran Desert toad is one of North America's largest toads and its skin makes a toxin to keep predators away.
where_to_find: Desert streams, washes and neighborhoods near the desert in Arizona.
spotting_tip: Never touch it. Look only with adult supervision.
safety_note: This toad's skin is toxic to pets. Do not touch; keep dogs away.

fun_fact: Spotted whiptails are very fast, darting lizards that are always on the move.
where_to_find: Desert grasslands, washes and canyons in southern Arizona.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny patches of dry ground for a quick, spotted striped lizard.

fun_fact: Southern cricket frogs make clicking calls that sound like two marbles tapped together.
where_to_find: Pond and stream edges with plants in the Southeast.
spotting_tip: Listen for clicks near shallow water and watch muddy edges from a distance.

fun_fact: Southern leopard frogs can leap many times their body length when startled.
where_to_find: Marshes, ponds, ditches and wet meadows in the South and Midwest.
spotting_tip: Listen for clucking calls near ponds and scan wet grass edges slowly.

fun_fact: Southern toads have bony ridges on their heads and sing long trills after rain.

spotting_tip: Check sunny rocks from a distance.

fun_fact: It drills neat rows of holes to drink tree sap.
where_to_find: Young woods and orchards.
spotting_tip: Look for rows of holes on tree trunks.

fun_fact: It has a red head and a pointed crest.
where_to_find: Parks, gardens and lawns.
spotting_tip: Check lawns for red-headed birds.

fun_fact: It feeds on crabs and crayfish.
where_to_find: Swamps, bayous and marshes.
spotting_tip: Scan marsh edges at dusk with an adult.

fun_fact: Its fuzzy coat keeps it warm in cold mountain air.
where_to_find: Meadows and tundra flowers.
spotting_tip: Watch wildflowers for fuzzy yellow bees.
safety_note: Bees can sting if bothered. Use zoom and give them space.

fun_fact: It sings a sweet song.
where_to_find: Gardens and open woods.
spotting_tip: Look in shrubs for yellow birds.

fun_fact: Males have a golden-yellow head.
where_to_find: Cattail marshes.
spotting_tip: Scan cattails from the shore.

fun_fact: Perch swim in schools.
where_to_find: Lakes and slow rivers.
spotting_tip: Look into clear water from docks.

fun_fact: It is quick and stores seeds.
where_to_find: Pine forests and sagebrush.
spotting_tip: Listen for chirps and watch logs.

fun_fact: Nicknamed the butter-butt for its yellow rump.
where_to_find: Woods, shrubs and backyards.
spotting_tip: Look for a flash of yellow on the rump.

fun_fact: It scuttles sideways.
where_to_find: Rocky shores and tide pools.
spotting_tip: Peer into tide pools from the edge.

fun_fact: Its yellow spots warn that it tastes bad.
where_to_find: Damp forest floors.
spotting_tip: Look on wet trails and leave logs where they are.
safety_note: Millipedes can make skin sore. Do not touch; wash hands if you do.

fun_fact: It cleans algae off reefs.
where_to_find: Coral reefs.
spotting_tip: Snorkel with an adult over shallow reefs.

fun_fact: Males and females look very different.
where_to_find: Wood edges and gardens.
spotting_tip: Check flowers on sunny days.

fun_fact: Its barred feathers look like zebra stripes.
where_to_find: Lawns and parks.
spotting_tip: Check lawns for small striped doves.

fun_fact: It uses a safety silk line when jumping.
where_to_find: Walls, fences and porches.
spotting_tip: Check sunny walls from a distance.

fun_fact: Zebra longwings roost in groups at night.
where_to_find: Gardens, wood edges and hammocks.
spotting_tip: Check flowers for long black-and-yellow striped wings.

fun_fact: It curls its tail up and runs fast.
where_to_find: Sandy desert flats.
spotting_tip: Watch sandy washes from a distance.

fun_fact: Black triggerfish look plain black until the light hits them, then a blue-green sheen and white lines along their fins show up.
where_to_find: Clear reef water along rocky Hawaiian shores; often seen from snorkel spots and piers.
spotting_tip: Look down from a pier or reef edge for dark, diamond-shaped fish with white lines at the base of the fins.

fun_fact: This little pufferfish is found only in Hawaii, and it can puff up its body when it feels threatened.
where_to_find: Shallow coral reefs and tide pools around the Hawaiian Islands.
spotting_tip: Watch small reef heads in calm, shallow water for a tiny brown fish covered in white spots.
safety_note: Pufferfish are poisonous to eat and can bite. Watch without touching and stay with an adult near the water.

size: 3.5 in long (9 cm) with a 11–13 in wingspan (28–33 cm)
fun_fact: Mexican free-tailed bats can fly over 99 mph, among the fastest flying speeds measured for any animal.
where_to_find: Warm southern states; huge colonies roost under bridges and in caves and fly out at sunset.
spotting_tip: Watch famous bat bridges or cave entrances at sunset, when long ribbons of bats stream out.
safety_note: Never touch a bat or pick one up from the ground; bats can carry rabies. Watch from a distance.

fun_fact: This butterflyfish gets its name from the dark mask across its eyes, like a raccoon's.
where_to_find: Coral and rocky reefs around Hawaii; often in small groups near ledges.
spotting_tip: Look for yellow fish with a black eye mask hovering near reef ledges.

size: Body 3–4 in across (8–10 cm) with spines up to 6 in (15 cm)
fun_fact: Its thick red spines are so blunt that people once used them like chalk pencils, which gave it its name.
where_to_find: Rocky reefs and surge zones along Hawaiian shores.
spotting_tip: Peer into reef cracks from above the water for bright red, pencil-thick spines.
safety_note: Don't step on or touch sea urchins. Wear water shoes and watch with an adult nearby.

size: 3.5–4.5 in long (9–11 cm) with a 11–12 in wingspan (28–31 cm)
fun_fact: Silver-haired bats get their name from the silvery tips on their dark fur that make them look frosted.
where_to_find: Forests across much of North America; they often roost under loose tree bark.
spotting_tip: Watch the sky over forest clearings and ponds at dusk for slow, low-flying bats.
safety_note: Never touch a bat or pick one up from the ground; bats can carry rabies. Watch from a distance.

fun_fact: Flying squirrels don't actually fly; they glide up to 150 ft between trees using furry skin stretched between their legs.
where_to_find: Woodlands across the eastern United States; they often visit bird feeders after dark.
spotting_tip: With an adult, watch a backyard bird feeder after dark with a dim red flashlight.

fun_fact: Boxfish have a hard, box-shaped shell made of fused bony plates, so they swim slowly by fluttering their small fins.
where_to_find: Coral reefs around Hawaii and the tropical Pacific.
spotting_tip: Look for a small dark fish covered in white spots that swims like a tiny box.
safety_note: Boxfish can release a toxin when stressed. Watch without touching and stay with an adult near the water.

fun_fact: A long thread trails from the back fin of this butterflyfish, which is how it got its name.
where_to_find: Shallow coral reefs around Hawaii.
spotting_tip: Look for white-and-yellow fish swimming in pairs over the reef, each with a thin thread behind its fin.

size: 28–32 in long incl. tail streamers (71–80 cm), wingspan about 3 ft (90 cm)
fun_fact: White-tailed tropicbirds have tail streamers almost as long as their bodies.
where_to_find: Sea cliffs and volcanic craters in Hawaii, such as the walls of Kīlauea.
spotting_tip: Scan cliff faces and crater walls for white birds with long tail streamers soaring on the wind.

fun_fact: The whitemouth moray opens and closes its mouth to breathe; it isn't being aggressive.
where_to_find: Coral and rocky reefs around Hawaii; usually peeking out of holes.
spotting_tip: Look into reef holes from a distance for a spotted eel's head with a white-lined mouth.
safety_note: Moray eels can bite hard. Never reach into holes or crevices; watch from a distance with an adult.

fun_fact: Goatfish use two whisker-like barbels under their chin to feel for food hidden in the sand.
where_to_find: Sandy patches next to reefs around Hawaii; often in big schools.
spotting_tip: Watch sandy bottoms near the reef for schools of fish with a yellow stripe down each side.

fun_fact: Zebra blennies are found only in Hawaii, and they hop between rocks in pools where waves splash.
where_to_find: Rocky tide pools and splash zones along Hawaiian shores.
spotting_tip: With an adult, watch a calm tide pool for a small striped fish perched on the rocks.
